issues.title: [M1][Results] Make Benchmark Result signing simple and vendor-friendly
issues.body:
## Goal

Define a simple, interoperable way to cryptographically sign SCAP-NG Benchmark Results so result authenticity and integrity are practical for vendors to implement.

## Motivation

Legacy SCAP/XML signature support has not translated into routine vendor signing of scan results. SCAP-NG should treat this as an interoperability and trust requirement, while avoiding XML Digital Signature complexity.

## Working requirements

- A Benchmark Result SHOULD be signable as a single logical artifact.
- Signing and verification SHALL use a deterministic/canonical byte representation.
- The normal signing path SHOULD NOT require XML Digital Signature processing.
- The signature mechanism SHOULD be implementable using widely available modern cryptographic libraries.
- The signed result SHALL identify the signature algorithm, signer/key identity, and verification material/reference needed by relying parties.
- Signature verification SHALL cover the Benchmark Result content needed to establish integrity, including embedded Rule Results and immutable references/digests to separately stored Assessment Results.
- If Assessment Results are external members of a result package, the signed Benchmark Result or signed result-package manifest SHALL cryptographically bind their digests.
- Signing SHALL NOT change assessment truth or scoring semantics.
- Verification failure SHALL be distinguishable from an unsigned result and from an otherwise valid assessment result.
- The design SHOULD support offline verification.
- Multiple signatures / organizational countersignatures MAY be supported only if they do not complicate the common one-signer case.

## Design directions to evaluate

1. Signed result-package manifest that binds Benchmark Result + Assessment Result member digests.
2. Detached signature over canonical Benchmark Result/package manifest bytes.
3. COSE/JWS-style envelopes or another compact modern signature format with a deliberately small required profile.

## Adoption principle

The default workflow should be roughly: serialize canonically -> sign bytes -> attach signature metadata -> verify bytes. If a scanner vendor needs a specialized XML-security stack or complex transform processing, the design has failed the simplicity objective.

## Relationship to legacy signatures

Legacy XML signatures encountered during migration may be verified/preserved as source provenance, but they do not define the SCAP-NG result-signing mechanism.

issues.title: [M2][Governance] Define SCAP-NG deprecation and removal lifecycle
issues.body:
## Purpose

Define a simple, predictable lifecycle for deprecating and eventually removing SCAP-NG constructs without recreating legacy compatibility debt.

This applies to native SCAP-NG and the standalone next-generation Assessment specification, including:

- Assessment capabilities/test types;
- fields/elements and enum values;
- result structures;
- authoring constructs;
- package/manifest features;
- conformance profiles;
- whole specification/schema versions.

## Design goals

- Deprecation SHALL be explicit and machine-readable where runtime/tooling behavior benefits from it.
- Deprecated features SHOULD remain valid only for a defined compatibility window; deprecation SHALL NOT imply indefinite support.
- New content SHOULD NOT use deprecated features.
- Validators/compilers SHOULD issue deterministic diagnostics identifying the deprecated construct, replacement (when one exists), and planned removal version/date if known.
- Scanners SHOULD be able to advertise which deprecated features they still support without requiring support forever.
- Conversion/migration tooling SHOULD provide a defined upgrade path where practical.
- Removal SHOULD occur only at an explicit specification-version boundary.
- A feature with no real-world use or no remaining semantic need SHOULD be removable rather than retained for hypothetical compatibility.
- Deprecation metadata SHALL NOT alter evaluation truth merely because a construct is deprecated.

## Questions to resolve

1. Where deprecation metadata lives: schema, capability registry, specification text, or a combination.
2. Whether every deprecated construct requires a replacement identifier or may be marked 'no replacement'.
3. Minimum compatibility window and whether time-based dates or version-based milestones are preferable.
4. Scanner conformance requirements for deprecated features.
5. How packages declare use of deprecated capabilities so scanners can reject early.
6. How result files report execution of deprecated constructs without polluting normal result semantics.
7. How migration tooling distinguishes deprecated-but-supported from removed/unsupported.
8. How Board/governance approval works for deprecation and removal.

## Working principle

Deprecation is a transition mechanism, not a permanent compatibility category. The standard should make removal possible and predictable.

issues.title: [M1][Manual] Define SCAP-NG Manual Assessment semantics using selected OCIL concepts
issues.body:
SCAP-NG currently has a deliberately minimal Manual Assessment model: stable identity, `mode: manual`, human-readable `procedure`, and a default operator-selected normalized outcome. That simplicity is useful, but the model is too loose for richer manual checks.

OCIL 2.0 is a valuable semantic source, but its XML object graph and authoring burden SHOULD NOT be copied wholesale.

## Recommended direction

Keep the current procedure-only Manual Assessment as the minimum valid form. Add an optional structured interaction layer inspired by OCIL.

### Preserve from OCIL

- typed questions: boolean, choice, numeric, string;
- explicit acceptable choices and reusable choice sets where useful;
- typed answer validation;
- explicit mapping from answers/ranges/patterns to normalized outcomes;
- ordered matching where overlap is possible;
- explicit handling of unknown / not_evaluated / not_applicable / error;
- optional branching to another declared interaction step/question;
- structured instructions/steps and references;
- provenance of the human answer/evaluator;
- machine-readable result independent of UI wording.

### Do not preserve by default

- OCIL's separate questionnaire/question/test_action object hierarchy when a compact inline form is sufficient;
- globally elaborate IDs for every private question/action node;
- XML-oriented indirection whose only purpose is serialization reuse;
- general workflow/programming behavior;
- implicit dynamic loading or arbitrary branching outside statically declared content.

## Proposed native model

A Manual Assessment MAY remain procedure-only:

```yaml
assessment:
  mode: manual
  procedure: |
    Review the configuration and determine compliance...
```

or MAY define structured interactions:

```yaml
assessment:
  mode: manual
  procedure: |
    Review the documented exception.
  questions:
    approved:
      type: boolean
      prompt: Is the exception formally approved?
    expiration:
      type: string
      prompt: Enter the approval expiration date.
  evaluate:
    ...
```

Exact syntax is undecided. The important architectural requirements are:

1. Procedure-only manual content remains valid and easy to author.
2. Structured questions are optional enhancements, not mandatory wrappers.
3. Manual interaction logic is declarative and statically visible.
4. Human answers remain observations; Organizational Input remains expected policy state.
5. Manual answer provenance is preserved in Assessment Results.
6. Branching MAY select another declared interaction step but SHALL NOT become a scripting language.
7. Conversion from XCCDF Check Text SHALL NOT invent structured questions.
8. Conversion from real OCIL MAY preserve structured semantics where present.

## Design questions

- Should the structured interaction layer support only one question per Manual Assessment initially, or arbitrary multi-question flows?
- Should branching be limited to questions within one Manual Assessment, or may it invoke another Manual Assessment?
- Should result mapping operate directly on typed answers, or through a separate expression/evaluate model?
- Are reusable choice groups worth preserving natively, or should the compiler deduplicate them?
- What exact answer/result domain should exist for unknown/not_evaluated/not_applicable/error?
- Should structured Manual Assessment remain SCAP-NG-native or eventually become an independent manual-interaction specification?

## Recommendation

Adopt a **two-tier Manual Assessment model**:

- Tier 1: minimal procedure + operator outcome (current model).
- Tier 2: optional typed structured interaction inspired by OCIL.

This retains authoring simplicity for the dominant STIG Check Text case while recovering the useful interoperability and validation semantics OCIL solved.

comments.body:
Refinement based on actual deployed OCIL usage:

The known OCIL content used operationally is generated from DISA Check Text, with response choices inserted to match DISA STIG Viewer behavior. The useful requirement is therefore traceable human determination, not general questionnaire/workflow expressiveness.

### Simplified recommendation

SCAP-NG Manual Assessment SHOULD avoid OCIL-style choose-your-own-adventure branching and stovepiped question/test-action/questionnaire graphs.

A Manual Assessment should normally contain:
- the authoritative human-readable procedure/check text;
- a very small declared response model;
- optional comments/evidence;
- normalized outcome mapping;
- evaluator identity;
- completion timestamp;
- source/import provenance when not entered directly.

Illustrative shape only:

```yaml
assessment:
  mode: manual
  procedure: |
    <publisher check text>
  response:
    type: stig_finding   # final vocabulary TBD
    choices:
      - compliant
      - finding
      - not_applicable
```

Result:

```yaml
manual_response:
  answer: finding
  outcome: fail
  completed_at: ...
  evaluator:
    id: ...
  comment: ...
  evidence_refs: []
```

The exact answer vocabulary should remain independent from normalized SCAP-NG outcomes so a DISA-oriented UI can present STIG Viewer terminology while another implementation can present different labels and still serialize the same interoperable result semantics.

Do not add arbitrary branching, nested questionnaire flows, or general workflow logic unless a concrete non-generated use case proves the need. If such a use case later appears, treat it as a new design decision rather than inheriting OCIL complexity by default.

### Traceability principle

A consumer should be able to answer from one Manual Assessment Result, without cross-document joins:
- what procedure was used;
- what answer the evaluator selected or supplied;
- what normalized outcome resulted;
- who made the determination;
- when it was made;
- what comments/evidence supported it;
- whether it was entered directly or imported.

This should follow the broader SCAP-NG result principle of avoiding stovepiped data layouts that require consumers to reconstruct meaning through unrelated object graphs.

Progress on the pre-schema-generation semantic gate:

### Resolved in current pre-alpha draft
- OVAL `extend_definition` -> statically declared Assessment-result dependency usable as an ordinary `evaluate` leaf; acyclic graph, full result-domain preservation, reuse/provenance rules.
- OVAL `applicability_check` -> intrinsic standalone Assessment applicability surface. False intrinsic applicability yields `not_applicable`; error/unknown/not_evaluated are not coerced. This remains distinct from SCAP-NG Rule `when` applicability.
- OVAL Results `variable_instance` -> distinct Assessment invocation/result identity for distinct effective bindings; source instance number retained only as migration provenance.
- XCCDF `complex-check` -> composed Assessment over dependent Assessment results; preserves recursive AND/OR/negate. Simple check `negate` is represented at the consuming expression, not by mutating the child Assessment.
- XCCDF `multi-check` and Rule `multiple` -> explicit Rule-result fan-out semantics; current direction is one policy-facing Rule Result with separately identifiable result instances plus deterministic aggregate Rule outcome.
- XCCDF grouped `requires` -> each source `requires` becomes one OR clause; repeated clauses are ANDed. Rule schema now supports explicit `any_of` clauses while retaining scalar shorthand during pre-alpha.

- `920ffd19` / `dfcf56ea`: Assessment-result dependencies and extend_definition mapping
- `7b73af38` / `9e01abcd`: dependent Assessment result provenance + fixture

issues.title: [Board Decision] Should the next-generation OVAL successor remain a standalone assessment standard?

comments.body:
Additional design point: `Assessment` is a role/concept, not a sufficient standards identity.

If the Board agrees that the OVAL successor remains standalone, the Board should also own the naming decision for that specification. The successor needs an explicit specification identity with at least:

- specification name;
- specification version;
- canonical schema/namespace identifier;
- conformance target/profile identifier where applicable;
- machine-readable declaration in content and results of the exact version used.

SCAP-NG should therefore reference the assessment specification by explicit identifier/version rather than merely saying `assessment`. Example conceptually:

```yaml
assessment_specification:
  id: <board-defined-name>
  version: <exact-version>
```

Likewise, scanner capability declarations should identify the exact assessment-spec versions/capabilities implemented.

This preserves product/version clarity while allowing `Assessment` to remain the generic document/component type.

Naming should remain a Board decision separate from the architectural vote. `OVAL 6` should remain excluded because that designation was already used by the prior unsuccessful effort.

issues.body:
## Purpose

Deferred design discussion: determine whether the XCCDF `Value` concept provides enough enduring value to justify a first-class SCAP-NG authoring construct, or whether it should exist only as a SCAP 1.4 migration concern.

This is **not current primary work** and SHALL NOT interrupt the present lossless-conversion/schema stabilization effort.

## Why revisit this

SCAP 1.4 XCCDF `Value` is useful for parameterizing some checks and tailoring, but its native datatype model is substantially narrower than the data model available to assessment engines such as OVAL.

Important correction/nuance: XCCDF 1.2 `Value` is not strictly string-only; it supports the XCCDF value types `string`, `number`, and `boolean` (plus selectors/choices and constraints). The underlying concern remains: this is not equivalent to the richer set of assessment datatypes and structures that SCAP-NG may need to bind into arbitrary Test/Collection/State/Variable inputs.

The current pinned NIWC corpus work also suggests that `Value` is relatively uncommon in newer content. Issue #45 found seven current packages whose conversion was blocked by XCCDF `Value`, and support was added so SCAP 1.4 conversion would remain lossless. That migration requirement does not by itself prove that the same abstraction belongs in the native NG authoring model.

## Questions for later review

1. **Usage census**
   - How many current NIWC/DISA benchmarks use XCCDF `Value`?
   - How many individual Values exist?
   - Which are still in actively maintained/recent benchmarks versus legacy content?
   - Which XCCDF types, selectors, bounds/patterns, refine-value and set-value features are actually used?

2. **Assessment binding coverage**
   - Which OVAL/NG input datatypes can existing XCCDF Values faithfully express?
   - Which cannot be represented without coercion or loss?
   - Can one Value bind safely to all assessment locations that legitimately need external/tailorable input?
   - How are lists, sets, records/structured values, binary/version/IP/time-like values, nullable values, and multi-valued inputs handled?

3. **Native design alternatives**
   Evaluate at least:
   - retain the current Parameter concept essentially as an XCCDF-compatible abstraction;
   - expand Parameters into a fully typed NG input model capable of representing every datatype/cardinality accepted by Assessment Tests/Collections/States/Variables;
   - remove XCCDF-style Values/Parameters from native authoring and translate the small legacy population during SCAP 1.4 conversion into ordinary typed assessment inputs/tailoring bindings.

4. **Tailoring semantics**
   Preserve the important distinction already made in NG design:
   - tailoring overrides a known requirement/input;
   - interactive/organizational input supplies a value when no universal requirement exists.
   
   Determine whether a generalized typed input mechanism can serve both without recreating unnecessary XCCDF complexity.

5. **Lossless migration**
   Regardless of the native decision, SCAP 1.4 → NG conversion SHALL preserve all valid XCCDF `Value`, `set-value`, `refine-value`, selector, constraint, and check-export semantics.
   Removing a native XCCDF-like abstraction would therefore require a deterministic conversion mapping and round-trip/equivalence evidence for the remaining legacy uses.

## Decision criteria

A first-class native Parameter/Value feature should remain only if it provides clear authoring/runtime value beyond migration compatibility.

If retained, it SHOULD be fully capable of representing the datatypes/cardinalities needed by native Assessment inputs rather than being a partial type island that works only for a subset of Tests.

If the real-world corpus shows very limited continued usage and a generalized typed Assessment-input mechanism subsumes the use cases cleanly, prefer conversion into that model rather than preserving XCCDF `Value` solely for historical familiarity.

## Relationships

- #22 — full XCCDF policy/profile/group/selector conversion gap audit.
- #45 — completed standards-valid corpus gap work that added lossless conversion support for XCCDF `Value`.
- #10 — OVAL variable/external-input/function equivalence.

## Explicit deferral

Do not make a native-language/schema decision from this issue yet. Revisit after:
- current v003 schema stabilization;
- full-corpus lossless conversion accounting is stable;
- the current corpus can be queried for actual `Value` usage patterns;
- the general typed Assessment input/variable model is mature enough for comparison.

comments.body:
Decision reached for native SCAP-NG Value/Parameter model:

- XCCDF `Value` does **not** survive as a native construct.
- SCAP-NG `Parameter` remains as typed policy-layer data independent of an Assessment.
- Assessment `Variable` remains execution/dataflow state inside the Assessment.
- `check-export` maps to an explicit typed Parameter -> Assessment input binding.
- Publisher Profiles may resolve publisher-defined Parameter variants.
- Organizational Input supplies a Parameter only when the publisher intentionally leaves the required value unresolved.
- Native Tailoring SHALL NOT override publisher-resolved Parameter values.
- If a publisher policy says X and an organization chooses Y, that is a distinct organization-authored policy/Benchmark, not a tailored evaluation of the unchanged publisher policy.
- Legacy XCCDF Tailoring value mutations therefore require a distinct local-policy migration representation (or fail closed until one is available), rather than becoming native Tailoring Parameter overrides.

Corpus evidence behind this decision: pinned NIWC Current contains 384 XCCDF Values across 7/65 packages, all on the scalar string/number/boolean surface, with 798 check-export bindings and no Profile value actions in that corpus. The bindings demonstrate the need for external policy data; they do not justify preserving the XCCDF Value abstraction itself.

Specification, Tailoring schema, and SCAP 1.4 crosswalk have been updated accordingly.

## Purpose

The pinned NIWC Current corpus contains several automated OVAL graphs that are XML/XSD-valid but fail stronger semantic/type validation. These appear to be **source-content defects**, not missing SCAP-NG capability.

The converter SHALL preserve the defect evidence, exclude only the affected automated Test/Assessment path, retain a verified manual source Assessment when available, and continue converting the rest of the Benchmark.

It SHALL NOT silently retag, coerce, or repair the invalid OVAL graph.

Pinned NIWC source revision:
`8c8e5dff860af6b1290ee9273a282db24278f8d5`

## Confirmed defect classes from the corpus run

### Invalid OVAL record datatype

Observed in:
- SQL Server 2016 Database — 1 affected Rule
- SQL Server 2016 Instance — 27 affected Rules / 54 blocked selector occurrences in evidence
- SQL Server 2022 Database — 1 affected Rule
- SQL Server 2022 Instance — 21 affected Rules / 42 blocked selector occurrences

Representative error:

```
invalid_oval_record_datatype
```

All affected Rules observed in the corpus artifact have usable manual Assessments.

### Test/Collection capability mismatch

Representative examples:

```
test_collection_capability_mismatch:windows.appcmd!=independent.variable
test_collection_capability_mismatch:unix.file!=independent.shellcommand
```

Observed in IIS 8.5 Site, IIS 10 Site, and F5 NGINX.

The NGINX case is the known class of source Test/Object mismatch that XML Schema alone does not catch.

### Filter/Collection capability mismatch

Representative errors:

```
Filter capability mismatch: get-all-vdir-paths-environment-variables-collection
Filter capability mismatch: get-all-vdir-paths-without-environment-variables-collection
```

Observed in IIS Site content.

## Required conversion behavior

For a **known, positively classified source semantic defect**:

1. Do not emit the invalid automated Assessment.
2. Record:
   - Rule ID;
   - selector;
   - source Definition/Test/Object/State IDs where available;
   - exact validation error;
   - classification `source_content_defect`;
   - source package/revision provenance.
3. If a verified source manual Assessment exists:
   - retain it;
   - if the invalid automated selector was the source/default selector, bind the native default to the manual Assessment;
   - record a `skipped_source_defect_manual_fallback` migration event.
4. Continue converting all unaffected Rules/Assessments in the Benchmark.
5. Do not claim automated round-trip equivalence for the excluded path.
6. If no usable manual fallback exists, keep the Rule/policy data but fail or mark the Rule unresolved according to the final Rule-without-executable-Assessment contract; do not invent a manual procedure.

## Safety

This mechanism SHALL use a narrow allowlist/classifier of errors that establish invalid source semantics. Unknown failures remain hard blockers.

Do not classify:
- unsupported but valid XCCDF/OVAL features;
- converter bugs;
- result mismatches;
- unresolved references that may be parser defects

as source defects merely to make a corpus pass.

## Current known cases to accept initially

- `invalid_oval_record_datatype`
- `test_collection_capability_mismatch:...`
- `Filter capability mismatch: ...`

Add additional classes only with source/schema/semantic evidence.

## Done when

- focused fixtures prove known source defects are quarantined and evidenced;
- unaffected content continues;
- manual fallback behavior is explicit;
- unknown errors still fail closed;
- SQL/IIS/NGINX packages are regenerated and their skipped automated Rules are enumerated;
- full-corpus accounting is rerun.

- Native Benchmark/Rule/Assessment/Collection source SHALL NOT be polluted with converter diagnostics, source-defect records, OVAL graph dumps, parity traces, skipped-Test details, or repository-normalizer lineage.
- Detailed migration evidence belongs in a separate evidence/report tree produced alongside conversion.
- Evidence may reference native logical IDs and source SCAP/OVAL IDs, but native content SHALL NOT need to reference the evidence in order to execute.
- Compiler/package input is the native content graph only. Migration evidence SHALL NOT be bundled into .scapng by default.

For source-defect quarantine specifically, evidence should contain Rule ID, source selector/Definition/Test/Object/State IDs where known, exact error, source package/revision, and fallback mapping. issues.title: [M2][Research, deferred] Assessment composition and shared runtime collection reuse
issues.body:
## Purpose

Research a possible future SCAP-NG Assessment-composition mechanism, conceptually similar to:

```yaml
include:
  - some-other-assessment.yaml
```

but **do not implement or alter the current native language yet**.

The motivating use case is that one Assessment may want to depend on or include
another Assessment so that Collections and derived observations can be reused:

- for authoring/code reuse;
- to avoid collecting the same system data repeatedly during one scan;
- to allow multiple Tests/Assessments to evaluate the same collected item set;
- to reduce duplicated detailed-result/evidence data in the NG analog of OVAL
  Results/System Characteristics.

This is deliberately deferred until lossless SCAP 1.4 → SCAP-NG conversion is
firmly stabilized. Research now; language/schema/runtime changes later.

## Conversion boundary

This feature is intended for **future native SCAP-NG authoring**, not as a
required or automatic SCAP 1.4 → SCAP-NG migration transform.

The XML/SCAP 1.4 converter SHALL:

- preserve the original source graph and semantics losslessly;
- NOT invent cross-Assessment dependencies merely because two converted
  Assessments happen to share equivalent Collections or observations;
- NOT rewrite ordinary converted content into composition constructs for
  optimization;
- preserve any source construct such as OVAL `extend_definition` according to
  its actual result-dependency semantics rather than translating it into a
  broader NG Collection-sharing feature.

After conversion, separate authoring/repository tooling MAY identify potential
composition/reuse opportunities for human review. The repository normalizer may
eventually suggest these opportunities, but automated migration SHALL remain
semantics-preserving and optimization-free.

This separation is important so lossless conversion proof does not depend on a
future NG-only authoring feature.

## Important distinction

This SHOULD NOT be designed as textual YAML preprocessing.

A literal `#include`/file splice would hide identity, dependency, provenance,
parameter binding and execution semantics.

If adopted, the feature should be a first-class Assessment dependency/composition
construct with stable logical IDs and explicit compiler/runtime semantics.

## Existing-model observations

### OVAL

OVAL `extend_definition` permits one Definition to reference/evaluate another
Definition's result within a logical criteria tree. This is useful prior art for
result-level composition, but it does **not** directly provide the richer
runtime model contemplated here: shared Collection instances/items reused by
multiple Tests/Assessments.

The SCAP-NG design must therefore distinguish:

- **result dependency/reuse** — Assessment A consumes the outcome of Assessment B;
- **collection reuse** — Assessment A and B consume the same runtime Collection
  execution/items;
- **definition/source reuse** — two Assessments reference the same authored
  Collection definition.

These are related but not equivalent.

### Other declarative systems

Static import/resolution models (for example OSCAL profile imports) are useful
prior art for explicit dependency resolution and deterministic compilation, but
do not by themselves define runtime observation sharing.

## Questions to research

### 1. Composition semantics

Should an Assessment be able to:

- invoke another whole Assessment and consume only its final result;
- consume named Tests from another Assessment;
- consume named Collections from another Assessment;
- consume named Variables/derived values from another Assessment;
- expose selected internal nodes as a stable public interface?

Avoid making every internal node globally addressable by accident.

### 2. Collection identity and execution reuse

If two Assessments reference the same Collection:

- what makes them the **same runtime Collection instance**?
- logical Collection ID?
- canonical semantic identity?
- Assessment-package identity + Collection ID?
- inputs/parameter bindings?
- target identity?
- behavior/evidence limits?

A shared collection can only be executed once if all result-affecting collection
inputs/behaviors are identical.

The runtime likely needs a cache key derived from:
- target;
- Collection semantic identity;
- bound inputs/variables;
- capability/version;
- collector behaviors/options.

### 3. Result graph

Detailed NG results should avoid copying identical collected items into each
Assessment result.

Potential model:

```text
scan
 ├─ collection-execution C1
 │    ├─ item I1
 │    └─ item I2
 ├─ assessment-execution A
 │    └─ test T1 -> references C1/I1/I2
 └─ assessment-execution B
      └─ test T9 -> references C1/I1/I2
```

This aligns with existing result-model direction that collected items are
first-class reusable result objects.

### 4. Execution DAG and cycle handling

Composition creates a dependency graph.

The compiler SHALL eventually need to detect and reject:
- direct include cycles;
- indirect Assessment dependency cycles;
- Collection/Variable dependency cycles introduced across Assessment boundaries.

The runtime should compile the resolved package into an execution DAG rather
than recursively interpreting source includes.

### 5. Parameter/input binding

If Assessment A depends on Assessment B:

- are B's parameters inherited?
- explicitly bound?
- renamed/aliased?
- allowed to use A's local Variables?
- allowed to expose derived Variables back to A?

Implicit lexical scope should be avoided.

Bindings should probably be explicit so identical imported Assessment logic with
different bindings can produce distinct execution instances.

### 6. Result semantics

If A consumes B's final result:
- preserve all six NG result values;
- define whether B error/unknown/not-applicable propagates and how;
- do not collapse B into Boolean.

If A only reuses B's Collection, B's own Test/result semantics should not
automatically affect A.

### 7. Short-circuiting and shared execution

A difficult case: Assessment A can logically short-circuit before a shared
Collection is needed, while Assessment B requires it.

Execution planning must not let one consumer's short-circuit decision suppress
data required by another consumer.

Conversely, the engine should not collect expensive data merely because an
unused dependent Assessment exists.

### 8. Evidence limits

Collection/evidence limits need careful separation.

A shared Collection may produce 1,000,000 items while:
- A evaluates until its truth is decisive;
- B needs the full population;
- each Rule retains only 50 decisive evidence records.

The shared runtime Collection record must distinguish actual collection
completeness from per-Test logical completeness and per-Rule evidence retention.

### 9. Security / sensitivity

Shared Collections must respect sensitive-result redaction. If any consumer
requires an item/entity value to remain redacted, shared result storage must not
leak it through another Assessment's evidence reference.

### 10. Packaging/compiler behavior

Authoring-time Assessment dependencies must be fully resolved by the content
compiler.

The final package manifest should contain immutable dependency bindings and
member digests. Runtime scanners SHALL NOT fetch arbitrary external YAML files
or resolve repository paths.

## Potential authoring direction — illustrative only

Do not treat this as accepted syntax:

```yaml
assessment:
  id: example.consumer

  dependencies:
    - assessment: ../shared/base-account-data.assessment.yaml
      as: account_data

  checks:
    privileged-accounts:
      collect:
        reuse: account_data.collections.local_accounts
```

A more constrained interface/export model may be preferable.

## Key design principle

**Share observations, not hidden mutable state.**

A Collection execution should be an immutable observation set for a given
target/input binding. Multiple Tests/Assessments may reference it, but one
consumer must not mutate the data seen by another.

## Relationship to Collection capability correction

This research reinforces the decision that Collection capability/type remains
first-class. A Collection that may be reused across Assessment boundaries must
remain self-describing independently of any one Test.

## Relationship to repository normalizer

The normalizer (#41) may eventually identify Assessments or Collections that are
good candidates for shared composition, but SHALL NOT invent cross-Assessment
dependencies automatically unless semantic equivalence and safe interface
contracts are proven.

## Relationship to detailed results

Issue #40 already proposes first-class reusable collected-item result objects.
This research may provide the execution/source model that naturally produces
that normalized result graph.

## Explicit deferral

**No current iteration-003/lossless-conversion source, schema, converter or
reference evaluator SHALL be changed to implement this feature yet.**

Research/documentation/prototypes may proceed in isolation only.

Revisit implementation after:
- lossless OVAL graph conversion semantics are stable;
- Collection/Test/State capability contracts are stable;
- detailed result identity/reuse model is drafted;
- compiler/package dependency resolution is defined.

## Research acceptance

Before any language change, produce:

1. OVAL `extend_definition` comparison and limitations;
2. at least three worked NG scenarios:
   - result-only Assessment dependency;
   - shared Collection consumed by two Tests;
   - shared Collection consumed by two different Assessments;
3. execution-DAG and cache-key proposal;
4. cycle/error semantics;
5. parameter/variable binding proposal;
6. normalized result/evidence example demonstrating actual size reduction;
7. security/redaction analysis;
8. migration analysis confirming that SCAP 1.4 → NG conversion remains
   lossless without inventing composition, and that composition is a
   native-authoring optimization/abstraction only;
9. Board-facing design question if the feature is proposed for the normative
   language.

comments.body:
## Research note — implications, benefits, risks, and guardrails

This research is intentionally **non-implementing**. It should inform the future native SCAP-NG schema after lossless SCAP 1.4 → NG conversion is stable.

### Prior-art observations

**OVAL `extend_definition`**
- OVAL already supports one Definition consuming another Definition's logical result.
- This validates result-level composition as a useful concept.
- It does **not** provide shared Collection execution, shared collected-item identity, or cross-Definition observation caching.
- Therefore SCAP-NG should not overload an `extend_definition` analog to mean Collection reuse.

Reference:
https://github.com/OVALProject/Language/blob/master/docs/oval-definitions-schema.md

**OSCAL Profile imports**
- OSCAL treats imports as explicit, resolvable dependencies rather than textual includes.
- Recursive imports create the possibility of circular dependency and therefore require explicit cycle handling.
- Import, merge, and modification are separate phases, which is a useful lesson for keeping dependency resolution separate from runtime evaluation.

Reference:
https://pages.nist.gov/OSCAL/learn/concepts/processing/profile-resolution/

**Bazel-style action caching**
- Safe reuse depends on an action having declared inputs and an identity derived from all execution-affecting inputs.
- Reusing output when a relevant input differs is incorrect, even when the source node appears to be the same.
- This is directly relevant to shared SCAP-NG Collection execution: Collection identity alone is insufficient; target, bound variables/parameters, capability/version, behaviors, and other collection-affecting inputs must participate in runtime identity.

Reference:
https://bazel.build/versions/7.1.0/remote/caching

---

## Potential benefits

### 1. Authoring reuse

A well-defined Assessment dependency/export mechanism could let authors implement a complex collection or derived observation once and reuse it from multiple Assessments.

This is especially valuable when multiple requirements inspect the same expensive source:
- local account inventories;
- installed packages;
- services;
- filesystem metadata;
- registry areas;
- certificates;
- security-policy exports;
- application configuration trees.

This could reduce copied logic and prevent separate implementations from drifting.

### 2. Runtime efficiency

The largest potential benefit is executing an expensive Collection once and allowing several Tests/Assessments to consume the immutable observation set.

Example:

```text
Collection: local_accounts
   ↓
Test A: privileged local accounts
Test B: disabled account policy
Test C: password age
Test D: orphaned account check
```

If collection inputs are identical, recollecting the same account inventory four times is unnecessary.

### 3. Smaller normalized result sets

A normalized NG result model can persist one Collection execution and one set of collected items, then let multiple Test executions reference them.

Instead of:

```text
A -> copy of accounts
B -> copy of accounts
C -> copy of accounts
```

use:

```text
CollectionExecution C1
  Items I1..In

TestExecution A -> C1
TestExecution B -> C1
TestExecution C -> C1
```

This could materially reduce the NG analog of OVAL Results/System Characteristics for large shared inventories.

### 4. Better provenance

One immutable Collection execution can have one acquisition timestamp/context and one collector diagnostic record. Multiple consumers then point to the same observation rather than producing subtly different duplicated evidence records.

### 5. Performance planning

An explicit dependency graph lets a scanner plan expensive work globally instead of evaluating each Assessment as an isolated recursive program.

The engine could:
- topologically order dependencies;
- collect once;
- fan results out to consumers;
- avoid work whose entire consumer set becomes unnecessary;
- parallelize independent Collections.

---

## Important risks

### 1. Hidden coupling

Assessment A can become fragile if it reaches arbitrarily into Assessment B's internals.

A future design SHOULD therefore expose an explicit public/export surface. Internal Collections, Variables, and Tests should remain private unless intentionally exported.

A construct such as:

```yaml
exports:
  collections:
    - local_accounts
```

may ultimately be safer than allowing arbitrary path references.

### 2. Cache-key unsoundness

Two references to the same authored Collection are **not necessarily the same runtime Collection execution**.

At minimum, runtime Collection identity may depend on:
- target identity;
- Collection semantic identity/version;
- capability and capability version;
- bound variables/parameters;
- collector behaviors/options;
- privilege/execution context where relevant;
- platform applicability context where it changes collection;
- possibly scanner/collector implementation compatibility.

If any collection-affecting input differs, the runtime must create distinct Collection executions.

### 3. Mutable/shared-state hazards

Consumers MUST NOT mutate a shared observation set.

The safe mental model is:

> Share immutable observations, not mutable execution state.

Tests derive results from Collection output; they do not alter the Collection for later consumers.

### 4. Dependency cycles

Cross-Assessment references can create cycles:

```text
A -> B -> C -> A
```

or subtler cycles through Variables/Collections.

The compiler should build a dependency DAG and reject cycles before packaging. Runtime recursion should never be the mechanism used to discover cycles.

### 5. Parameter/variable scope leakage

Implicit parent/child scope would make composition difficult to reason about and difficult to cache correctly.

Bindings should be explicit. A dependent Assessment should not automatically inherit all variables from its caller.

Likely rule:
- imported/dependent nodes receive only explicitly bound inputs;
- exported results/Collections are explicitly named;
- no implicit lexical variable capture.

### 6. Result dependency versus Collection dependency confusion

These must remain separate:

- **Assessment-result dependency:** A consumes B's final six-valued result.
- **Test/result dependency:** A consumes a named Test result.
- **Collection dependency:** A consumes B's collected observation set.
- **source reuse:** A and B happen to reference the same Collection definition.

Each has different propagation and execution semantics.

### 7. Six-valued truth propagation

If an Assessment consumes another Assessment's result, `error`, `unknown`,
`not_evaluated`, and `not_applicable` must remain first-class.

Composition must not silently Booleanize the dependency.

Collection reuse, on the other hand, should not inherit the producer Assessment's final truth result at all.

### 8. Short-circuit interaction

One Test may reach a decisive result without requiring the complete shared Collection, while another consumer may require the full population.

Therefore:
- per-Test logical completeness;
- Collection population completeness;
- retained evidence completeness

must remain separate.

A consumer's short-circuit must never truncate data required by another live consumer.

### 9. Evidence-cap interaction

Evidence caps are per result/reporting requirement, not necessarily per Collection execution.

A single complete Collection may support:
- Test A retaining 10 decisive failures;
- Test B retaining 50 examples;
- Test C retaining no item detail.

The engine should not recollect or duplicate observations solely because evidence-retention policies differ.

### 10. Sensitive-data/redaction interaction

If a shared Collection contains sensitive values, one consumer must not be able
to disclose a value that another governing collection/redaction contract marks sensitive.

Conservative rule candidate:
- redaction is attached to the observation/entity disclosure contract;
- shared storage retains the strongest applicable redaction requirement;
- consumer-specific evidence rendering cannot weaken it.

### 11. Versioning and interface stability

Once an Assessment exports a Collection for other Assessments to consume, that
Collection's shape becomes an interface.

Changing:
- field names;
- datatypes;
- cardinality;
- capability;
- parameter contract

can become a breaking change for downstream Assessments.

This argues for explicit exported-interface versioning or compiler compatibility checks.

### 12. Debugging complexity

Shared execution improves efficiency but can make failures harder to trace.

Developer results should make it obvious:
- which Collection execution a Test used;
- why that execution was shared;
- which bindings formed its execution identity;
- which Assessments/Tests consumed it;
- whether it was complete/cached/reused;
- where collection errors originated.

---

## Design guardrails worth carrying forward

1. **No textual YAML include semantics.**
2. **No implementation in the lossless converter.**
3. **Compiler resolves the full dependency graph before package creation.**
4. **Runtime sees immutable manifest-bound dependencies, never arbitrary filesystem paths.**
5. **Collections remain independently typed/self-describing.**
6. **Only explicitly exported nodes may be consumed across Assessment boundaries.**
7. **Bindings are explicit; no implicit variable scope capture.**
8. **Runtime Collection reuse requires an exact execution-identity match.**
9. **Cycles are compile-time errors.**
10. **Shared observations are immutable.**
11. **Assessment-result dependency and Collection reuse remain distinct concepts.**
12. **Result normalization stores shared collected items once and references them by stable execution/item IDs.**
13. **Redaction is never weakened by reuse.**
14. **Evidence caps do not define Collection completeness.**
15. **The feature remains optional for native authoring; ordinary Assessments remain fully valid without composition.**

---

## Suggested future schema shape

Do not adopt this syntax yet; this is only to make the research concrete.

A safer model than `#include` may be an explicit dependency/import plus exports:

```yaml
assessment:
  id: account-policy

  dependencies:
    account_inventory:
      assessment: ../shared/account-inventory.assessment.yaml
      version: 1

  checks:
    privileged-accounts:
      collect:
        from: account_inventory
        collection: local_accounts
```

Producer:

```yaml
assessment:
  id: account-inventory

  exports:
    collections:
      local_accounts:
        collection: local_accounts
        interface_version: 1
```

This allows the compiler to validate that:
- the export exists;
- capability/type matches the consumer;
- interface version is compatible;
- all required bindings are supplied;
- no dependency cycle exists.

Again, syntax is intentionally **not proposed for implementation yet**.

---

## Recommendation from this research

Keep this issue deferred until the current lossless-conversion work is stable, but reserve architectural space for the feature in the future schema.

When revisited, prototype **Collection reuse first**, before whole-Assessment result composition. Collection reuse provides the clearest measurable benefit (authoring reuse, collection efficiency, normalized results) while introducing fewer truth-propagation semantics than Assessment-result composition.

Do not optimize converted SCAP 1.4 content into this form automatically. If useful, future repository-normalizer tooling can identify candidate reuse after conversion for human review.

comments.body:
Follow-up design observation: Collection reuse may eventually have a legitimate SCAP 1.4 → NG conversion role, even though it should NOT be implemented during the current lossless-conversion stabilization phase.

Reason: monolithic OVAL content already permits one Object to be referenced by multiple Tests and by larger Variable/Set/Filter dependency graphs. In practice, shared Objects are common. Our current per-Rule split/conversion model can therefore duplicate source Objects into multiple native Assessments even when the original OVAL graph contained one shared Object identity.

This suggests a possible later conversion refinement:

1. First complete and prove the current lossless conversion using the explicit per-Rule/native Assessment model.
2. Preserve source OVAL graph identity/provenance strongly enough to know when multiple converted Collections originate from the same source Object (or provably equivalent resolved Object graph).
3. In a later, separately validated converter mode/pass, emit one shared native NG Collection and have multiple Assessments reference it.
4. Do NOT infer sharing merely from similar YAML or filenames. Prefer exact source identity first; semantic-equivalence-based consolidation belongs to repository-normalizer/human-review territory.
5. Keep source-definition/result dependency (e.g. extend_definition) separate from Object/Collection reuse.
6. Prove that parameter/variable bindings, behaviors, filters, sets and any collection-affecting context are equivalent before treating multiple consumers as one runtime Collection execution.
7. Preserve the ability to round-trip or explain source provenance: reviewers should be able to see that several NG Assessment references trace back to one OVAL Object/dependency node.

This would align NG Collection reuse with an existing OVAL capability rather than treating it solely as a new optimization.

Important boundary: this is a **later design-change candidate**, not authorization to modify the current converter. The current priority remains stabilization and proof of lossless conversion.

comments.body:
Design discussion: imported Collection/item reuse and per-Assessment result completeness

A useful distinction emerged for future Assessment composition/shared Collection reuse:

**Reuse the collection execution, but materialize imported observations into the consuming Assessment's result namespace.**

Example:
- Assessment A executes Collection C and produces Items 1-500.
- Assessment B imports/reuses C rather than gathering the same system data again.
- When B's standalone result is serialized, B should include its own local representation of those imported Items first (for example Items 1-500 in B's result namespace), then assign IDs 501-N to Items collected uniquely by B.
- B's Tests reference B-local item IDs, not opaque IDs that only exist in A's result document.

This is intentionally less storage-efficient than a globally normalized result graph, but it preserves a crucial property: **an Assessment result single is coherent and self-contained when saved, transported, or reviewed independently.**

If reused Items were stored only in the originating Assessment's result:
- B's Test results would contain references that cannot be understood without separately locating/loading A's result;
- exported/saved Assessment singles would not be complete;
- ordering/retention/lifecycle dependencies between Assessment result files would appear;
- external consumers such as Splunk or evidence-review tooling would have to reconstruct cross-file joins merely to explain why one Test passed or failed.

The proposed semantics are therefore:

1. **Collection execution identity** may be shared across Assessments at runtime to avoid duplicate gathering.
2. **Collected Item values** are immutable observations from that shared execution.
3. Each consuming Assessment result imports/materializes the observations it actually uses into its own result namespace.
4. Imported Items preserve provenance back to the originating shared Collection execution (e.g. source collection execution ID / digest / originating Assessment if relevant), but their local result IDs are scoped to the consuming Assessment result.
5. Items unique to the consuming Assessment are numbered/identified after imported Items under a deterministic ordering rule.
6. Tests always reference Items available inside the same serialized Assessment result.
7. Evidence caps/retention rules must distinguish:
   - Items available from the shared runtime Collection;
   - Items imported/materialized into a specific Assessment result;
   - smaller decisive evidence subsets retained for individual Test/Rule reporting.

This gives us two representations with different optimization goals:
- **runtime:** normalized/shared Collection execution and immutable observation sets;
- **serialized Assessment single:** self-contained imported copies sufficient to make that Assessment's Tests/results intelligible on their own.

A future whole-scan/enterprise result format MAY additionally normalize shared observations globally to avoid duplication across many Assessment results, but that optimization should not make an individual Assessment result dependent on another Assessment result file.

Open questions to resolve later:
- whether imported item IDs should be simple sequential local IDs, stable content-derived IDs, or both;
- exact provenance fields linking imported local Items to the shared Collection execution;
- whether all collected Items are imported or only Items actually required to support the consuming Assessment's evaluation/evidence;
- how truncated collection/evidence states are represented when one Assessment needs more of the shared Collection than another;
- whether a standalone Assessment result SHALL always be independently interpretable without external result files.

This direction appears compatible with the earlier principle: **share observations at runtime, not hidden mutable state**, while keeping serialized Assessment results coherent and portable.

issues.title: [M2][Research, non-voting] OVAL mask → SCAP-NG sensitive-result redaction divergence
issues.body:
## Purpose

Document and research a proposed intentional divergence from OVAL 5.12.3 for
eventual OVAL Board review.

OVAL exposes a generic entity/field `mask` attribute with default `false`.
When effective `mask=true`, the corresponding collected value is suppressed
from OVAL Results/System Characteristics output for sensitivity reasons.

Current SCAP-NG design direction is **not** to carry this generic `mask`
property onto every native Object/State/entity/predicate. Instead, NG would
preserve the underlying security behavior through a narrower explicit
**sensitive-result redaction** construct used only where collected values should
not be disclosed in detailed results.

This issue is **research/non-voting**. It should lead to a separate GitHub
Discussion labeled for Board vote once corpus evidence and the proposed NG
syntax/semantics are complete.

## Why this is being reconsidered

During RHEL 9 and Windows 11 native-content review, converted Assessments showed
large numbers of `mask: false` fields. These were not generally explicit
publisher choices; they were materialized from the OVAL XSD default.

The practical value of exposing a generic `mask` property in native NG
authoring is unclear. A clear use case exists for sensitive data such as UNIX
password/shadow/hash collection, where the evaluator may need the value but
results should not disclose it. Broader real-world usage has not yet been
demonstrated.

SCAP-NG should preserve necessary redaction behavior without carrying legacy
surface area that provides little author value.

## Authoritative OVAL behavior to preserve

Pinned OVAL 5.12.3 schemas define:

- `mask` as optional with default `false`;
- `mask=true` as an instruction that corresponding sensitive collected values
  MUST NOT appear in the Results copy of System Characteristics;
- conflicting masking requirements resolve conservatively toward masking.

The proposed NG divergence concerns **authoring representation and scope**, not
removal of sensitive-result protection.

## Research required before Board vote

Perform a corpus census of **source-explicit** `mask=true` and
`mask=false` across:

- pinned NIWC RHEL 9 content;
- pinned NIWC Windows 11 content;
- the broader NIWC Current corpus;
- representative upstream/community OVAL content where available.

ZIP/datastream contents must be inspected directly; GitHub indexed code search
is insufficient.

For every explicit use, record:

- benchmark/platform;
- Rule/Definition/Test capability family;
- Object/State/entity/field location;
- true vs false;
- whether the value is plausibly sensitive;
- whether masking is necessary for result confidentiality;
- whether an equivalent narrow NG redaction construct would preserve behavior.

## Proposed SCAP-NG direction

Subject to corpus evidence:

1. Native NG SHALL NOT require or expose generic `mask: false` on ordinary
   assessment predicates.
2. NG SHOULD define an explicit sensitive-result redaction mechanism only where
   an Assessment actually requires value suppression.
3. Converted OVAL `mask=true` MUST preserve equivalent redaction behavior.
4. OVAL explicit/default provenance SHOULD remain available in migration
   evidence even when `mask=false` is omitted from normalized NG source.
5. Conflicting redaction requirements SHALL resolve toward redaction.
6. Detailed NG results SHALL be able to state that a value was collected and
   intentionally redacted without disclosing the value.
7. Redaction is independent of evidence truncation/capping.
8. The conversion tool SHALL document this as an intentional SCAP 1.4 → NG
   representation divergence.

## Proposed future Board-vote Discussion wording

> **[VOTE] Do you agree with updating SCAP-NG to replace OVAL's generic entity/field `mask` property with a narrower explicit sensitive-result redaction mechanism, while preserving equivalent redaction behavior for converted `mask=true` content and omitting default/inherited `mask=false` from native NG authoring?**

Before opening that vote, attach:

- corpus census results;
- proposed NG syntax and JSON Schema;
- conversion examples;
- detailed-result examples;
- compatibility crosswalk entry;
- known consequences for SCAP 1.4 round-trip conversion.

## Round-trip consequence

If NG omits generic default `mask=false`, backward conversion to OVAL can
reconstruct the effective OVAL default `false` without changing semantics.

If NG uses a narrower explicit redaction construct, forward conversion of
`mask=true` SHALL map to it. Backward conversion from that construct SHOULD
emit OVAL `mask=true` where OVAL supports an equivalent location.

Exact byte/attribute-presence round trip is therefore not a goal; semantic
redaction behavior is.

## Related issues

- #8 OVAL XSD default/inherited-behavior audit
- #9 importer effective-default and explicitness provenance
- #25 native specification/glossary/SCAP 1.4 compatibility crosswalk
- #40 detailed Assessment/Test/collected-item result schemas

## Exit criteria

This research issue is ready to hand off to a Board vote when:

- explicit-mask corpus census is complete;
- NG redaction syntax/semantics are drafted;
- conversion and result examples exist;
- compatibility/round-trip consequences are documented;
- the final vote wording is frozen.

issues.title: [M2] Open-source SCAP-NG content compiler, bundle builder and signer
issues.body:
## Purpose

Create an open-source SCAP-NG **content compiler** that takes native authoring
YAML (Benchmark, Rule, Assessment, applicability, profiles/tailoring inputs and
shared Assessments), validates and resolves it, builds the deterministic NG
distribution bundle and manifest, and optionally digitally signs the compiled
artifact.

This is the companion tool to the repository normalizer. The normalizer
maintains authoring repositories; the compiler turns a valid authoring tree
into a portable scanner-consumable SCAP-NG package.

## Primary workflow

Conceptually:

```text
native authoring YAML
    ↓
validate schemas + authoring contracts
    ↓
resolve Benchmark → Rule → selected/shared Assessment graph
    ↓
freeze identities/versions/references
    ↓
construct deterministic package manifest
    ↓
emit reproducible NG bundle
    ↓
digitally sign bundle/manifest
    ↓
verify signature + package integrity
```

Compilation SHALL NOT depend on repository-relative paths at runtime. Relative
authoring references are resolved during compilation into immutable packaged
members and manifest bindings.

## Required compiler behavior

The compiler SHALL:

1. Discover and validate all native SCAP-NG source files using the applicable
   versioned JSON Schemas and semantic validation rules.
2. Resolve every Benchmark → Rule → Assessment and applicability reference,
   including shared Assessments.
3. Reject unresolved references, conflicting logical identities, wrong object
   types, source-boundary escapes and unsupported/deprecated constructs.
4. Resolve Profiles/Tailoring/parameters sufficiently to validate all published
   references without silently changing their semantics.
5. Preserve logical IDs independently from authoring file paths.
6. Produce a deterministic package member layout and deterministic manifest.
7. Record each packaged object's logical identity, type, version, immutable
   member path, content digest and size.
8. Record package/content schema versions and compiler version/provenance.
9. Record source provenance sufficient to reproduce the build when supplied by
   the authoring repository/build environment.
10. Ensure all manifest digests are computed over the exact bytes packaged.
11. Support reproducible builds: identical normalized inputs and compiler
    configuration SHOULD produce byte-identical unsigned bundles.
12. Validate the completed bundle before signing.
13. After signing, verify the signature and all package/member digests before
    reporting success.
14. Never modify source authoring files as a side effect of compilation.

## Bundle format

The final serialization is still pre-alpha, but the compiler SHOULD produce one
portable archive containing at minimum:

- `manifest.json` (or the finally selected canonical manifest serialization);
- compiled Benchmark object(s);
- Rule objects;
- Assessment objects, including shared Assessments;
- applicability objects;
- any required profile/tailoring material;
- optional metadata/provenance members;
- the detached or embedded package signature material selected by the final
  signing design.

The manifest SHALL be scanner-authoritative for runtime object resolution.
Scanners SHALL NOT infer members from filenames or directory conventions.

## Signing requirements

The compiler SHALL support at least two signing backends:

### 1. Software certificate/private key

For CI, development and environments using file-backed credentials, support a
software X.509 certificate and private key. The implementation SHOULD support
common PEM/PKCS#12 inputs as appropriate and SHALL avoid exposing private-key
material in logs.

Encrypted keys SHALL use secure password input; plaintext passwords SHALL NOT
be required on the command line.

### 2. PKCS#11 smart card / token / HSM

Support signing through PKCS#11 so a private key can remain on a CAC/PIV smart
card, hardware token or HSM.

The implementation SHOULD prefer a maintained, general-purpose Python signing
stack over copying SCAP/XML-specific NIWC signing code.

Current candidate stack to evaluate:

- `python-pkcs11` for high-level PKCS#11 access to HSM/smart-card devices;
- `pyHanko` generic CMS signing APIs, which provide both a software
  `SimpleSigner` and a `PKCS11Signer` and can produce detached CMS signatures
  over arbitrary byte streams.

This combination is attractive because the same signature envelope can be used
whether the private key is file-backed or hardware-backed, while the private-key
operation remains isolated behind the signer backend.

The existing NIWC public-domain implementation at
`niwc-atlantic/scap-content-library/scripts/p11xs.py` remains useful prior art
for CAC/PIV/OpenSC deployment experience, certificate/key selection, PIN
handling and PKCS#11 interoperability. It SHOULD be consulted for lessons
learned and fallback implementation details, but SHALL NOT be treated as the
preferred implementation merely because it already exists. Its XML-DSig/XAdES
layer is not relevant to the SCAP-NG bundle signature format.

A provenance entry SHOULD record any NIWC logic that is actually copied or
adapted. If no NIWC code is reused, the compiler SHOULD simply document it as
reviewed prior art rather than inherited implementation.

## Signature design requirements

The exact SCAP-NG signature envelope/algorithm profile remains a design item,
but the implementation SHALL follow these principles:

1. Sign canonical package integrity material rather than authoring paths.
2. The signature SHALL cryptographically bind the immutable manifest and,
   transitively, every packaged member digest.
3. Verification SHALL detect member modification, removal, substitution or
   manifest replacement.
4. The signer certificate/chain and signature algorithm identifiers SHALL be
   available to the verifier.
5. Signing SHALL NOT require the scanner to understand PKCS#11; PKCS#11 is a
   compiler-side private-key interface only.
6. Signature creation and verification SHOULD be modular so algorithm/profile
   changes do not alter the compiler's content-resolution logic.
7. The first implementation SHOULD support an X.509-friendly, standards-based
   detached signature profile with algorithm agility. RSA/SHA-256 is a useful
   initial interoperability target for current CAC/PIV/PKCS#11 environments,
   but SHALL NOT be selected merely to match the legacy NIWC XML signer.
8. Compiler signing SHALL fail closed: no “signed” package may be emitted if
   post-sign verification fails.

## CLI concept

Illustrative only:

```text
scap-ng compile source/ --output benchmark.scapng

scap-ng compile source/ --output benchmark.scapng \
    --sign software --cert signer.pem --key signer-key.pem

scap-ng compile source/ --output benchmark.scapng \
    --sign pkcs11 \
    --pkcs11-module /path/to/provider \
    --cert-id <id>

scap-ng verify benchmark.scapng
```

A `--validate-only` mode SHOULD run the full pre-package validation/resolution
pipeline without emitting a bundle.

## Manifest / reproducibility details

The manifest SHOULD include or bind:

- package format/schema version;
- package ID/version;
- compiler name/version;
- content object inventory;
- logical IDs and versions;
- object type;
- member path;
- digest algorithm + digest;
- byte length;
- required capability/schema versions where applicable;
- build provenance that does not make otherwise reproducible content
  nondeterministic.

Timestamps, if required for provenance, SHALL be separated from deterministic
content identity or handled in a defined reproducible-build model.

The package's immutable identity SHOULD be content-derived from canonical
manifest/integrity material.

## Relationship to authoring repository normalizer

The repository normalizer and compiler have deliberately separate roles:

- **normalizer:** discovers duplicate/near-duplicate Assessments and improves
  source reuse/layout;
- **compiler:** validates and freezes whatever valid authoring graph it receives,
  creates the deterministic package/manifest, and signs it.

The compiler SHALL NOT silently normalize or merge author content.

## Testing / acceptance

Initial acceptance SHOULD include:

- compile the current RHEL 9 iteration-003 review;
- compile the current Windows 11 iteration-003 review, including its explicit
  deprecated-test/manual fallback;
- package both with deterministic manifests;
- verify every manifest/member digest;
- build the same unsigned input twice and compare bundle identity/bytes;
- sign and verify using a software test certificate;
- sign and verify using a PKCS#11 software token in CI where practical;
- manually validate a physical smart-card/CAC/PIV path;
- negative tests for modified manifest, modified member, missing member,
  substituted member, wrong certificate and invalid signature;
- ensure private key/PIN material never appears in logs.

## Open-source deliverable

Publish the compiler and verifier under the repository tooling area with:

- documented CLI;
- versioned manifest/package contract;
- software signing backend;
- PKCS#11 signing backend using a maintained general-purpose library where practical;
- standards-based detached signature verifier;
- provenance ledger identifying any reused/adapted NIWC logic, or noting it as reviewed prior art when none is copied;
- automated tests and example GitHub Actions workflows.

comments.body:
Decision note — signing implementation direction confirmed:

- Prefer a maintained general-purpose Python signing stack over copying the NIWC XML signer.
- Evaluate `pyHanko` detached CMS signing for arbitrary manifest bytes, using its software `SimpleSigner` and PKCS#11-backed `PKCS11Signer`.
- Use `python-pkcs11` for smart-card/HSM access where appropriate.
- Keep one standards-based signature envelope regardless of whether the private key is file-backed or hardware-backed.
- Treat NIWC `scripts/p11xs.py` as reviewed prior art for CAC/PIV/OpenSC/PKCS#11 operational lessons only, unless a concrete library gap requires code reuse.
- Do not carry XML-DSig/XAdES assumptions into the SCAP-NG bundle signature design.
- Keep algorithm agility; RSA/SHA-256 is only an initial interoperability target, not a legacy constraint.

This is already reflected in the issue body; this comment records the explicit project decision for future traceability.

comments.body:
Package-layout review finding from the full pinned native normalizer experiment:

The current compiler flattens every referenced Assessment into `objects/assessments/<assessment-id>.json` regardless of whether the authoring source was under `assessments/automated/`, `assessments/manual/`, `assessments/applicability/`, or the repository-level shared Assessment area.

This loses useful structural distinctions that remain explicit in the native authoring tree.

Track as a compiler/package-layout gap. Before changing serialization, define a deterministic package hierarchy that preserves at least:
- Assessment mode/category: automated, manual, applicability;
- local vs repository-shared provenance/placement;
- logical identity independent of member path.

A candidate layout for discussion is:
- `objects/assessments/automated/`
- `objects/assessments/manual/`
- `objects/assessments/applicability/`
- `objects/assessments/shared/automated/`
- `objects/assessments/shared/manual/`
- `objects/assessments/shared/applicability/` if shared applicability Assessments are permitted.

The manifest remains scanner-authoritative; these paths are for human reviewability and package organization, not semantic identity.

Do not finalize the exact hierarchy until shared Assessment naming/identity discussion in #41 is resolved.

comments.body:
Design decision: the compiled package layout SHOULD mirror the native authoring layout wherever practical for human debugging and review.

Rationale:
- a reviewer should be able to move from an authoring path to the corresponding packaged object without learning a second taxonomy;
- automated/manual/applicability distinctions remain visible after compilation;
- local vs shared Assessment placement remains obvious;
- package diffs are easier to reason about;
- support/debugging can compare source and bundle trees directly.

The manifest remains authoritative for runtime resolution and logical identity. Directory structure is therefore not a scanner semantic dependency, but the compiler SHOULD preserve the authoring taxonomy unless compilation has a concrete reason to transform it.

Current target direction:

Authoring:
- `assessments/automated/`
- `assessments/manual/`
- `assessments/applicability/`
- repository `shared/assessments/automated/`
- repository `shared/assessments/manual/`
- repository `shared/assessments/applicability/` where applicable

Compiled bundle:
- `objects/assessments/automated/`
- `objects/assessments/manual/`
- `objects/assessments/applicability/`
- `objects/shared/assessments/automated/`
- `objects/shared/assessments/manual/`
- `objects/shared/assessments/applicability/` where applicable

Prefer this mirroring principle for other object classes as the package model grows (for example rules, tailoring, organizational inputs, and future result-supporting metadata), while keeping paths non-semantic and manifest-controlled.

Add regression coverage that compares authoring classification/placement with packaged placement so future compiler refactors cannot silently flatten the tree again.

- benchmark: 22,692 raw -> 4,239 compressed
- applicability: 1,855 raw -> 377 compressed

The compiler is already using ZIP DEFLATE with compresslevel=9. The poor aggregate ratio is therefore not a low compression setting. ZIP compresses each member independently, resetting the dictionary on every small JSON file, and incurs per-member headers/central-directory overhead.

Control experiment over the exact extracted RHEL 9 NG payload:
- concatenate all member bytes and zlib level 9: ~308,915 bytes
- same tree as tar.gz level 9: ~372,044 bytes

That is strikingly close to the user's ~384 KB legacy SCAP 1.4 ZIP, despite the NG expanded payload being of similar magnitude. This strongly indicates package granularity/solid-compression behavior is the dominant reason the current .scapng is ~1.07 MB.

Design implication: do not optimize native semantics merely to chase bundle size until package representation is tested. Evaluate at least:
1. keep human-debuggable source/package taxonomy but aggregate objects into a small number of canonical JSON members by class/category before archive compression;
2. use a solid-compression container (e.g. tar+gzip or tar+zstd) while retaining manifest member indexes/digests;
3. investigate ZIP/Zstandard, noting that per-file compression still loses cross-file dictionary reuse unless dictionary/shared-stream support is introduced;
4. measure reproducibility, random-access needs, signing/integrity behavior, scanner startup cost, and tooling interoperability for each option.

Important: preserve the earlier source/package mirroring principle at the *logical* object-path level even if physical serialization groups objects into larger members. The manifest can map logical object paths/IDs to offsets or aggregate member locations.

Add a package-format benchmark regression using this exact RHEL 9 corpus so future format experiments compare raw bytes, archive bytes, entry count, startup/read costs, and reproducibility against this baseline.

comments.body:
Security correction / scanner trust model:

A cached SHA-256 of the .scapng package proves only that the package file is unchanged. It does **not** prove that a previously extracted cache of thousands of files remains identical to the verified package. Because an SCAP-NG scanner may run as root and may support high-impact assessment capabilities such as shell-command and SQL execution, an independently mutable extracted tree MUST NOT be trusted merely because the source package hash is unchanged.

For high-assurance execution, one of these models is required:

### Preferred baseline: immutable package is the execution trust anchor
- Install the signed .scapng as one immutable package file.
- Initial install/update: validate publisher signature, manifest, and all member digests.
- Cache the verified whole-package SHA-256/trust record.
- Before each scan, hash the single .scapng file.
- If unchanged, parse/read Assessment content directly from the verified archive, or extract only into ephemeral memory/private scratch for that scan.
- Persistent extracted files SHALL NOT become authoritative executable content.

This preserves the SCAP 1.4-style one-file cheap change detector and ensures bytes interpreted/executed by the scanner come from the cryptographically trusted package.

### If persistent extraction is required
Simply storing files under root ownership/read-only permissions is insufficient for cryptographic assurance. The scanner would need either:
- verify every consumed member against its signed-manifest digest before use (lazy verification can avoid hashing files never used); or
- store the extracted image under a cryptographically verified filesystem/container mechanism such as a Merkle-tree-backed read-only image (e.g. fs-verity per-file or a dm-verity-style whole-image design), with the trusted root hash bound to the verified package identity.

A particularly relevant package/runtime option is a single compressed tar/solid payload or read-only filesystem image whose one content hash/Merkle root is authenticated by the signed manifest. This could preserve human-readable logical paths while giving the scanner one trusted storage object rather than 1,000+ mutable filesystem objects.

### Cached compiled representation
If the scanner creates a persistent parsed/compiled execution plan for performance, that cache is also executable/trusted content. It SHALL either:
- be regenerated from the verified package for each process/run;
- be stored as one canonical serialized object whose digest is cryptographically tied to the verified package digest and rechecked before use; or
- reside inside an authenticated read-only storage image.

### Threat-model requirement
For privileged scanners, no content capable of influencing command/SQL/query execution may be consumed from a persistent cache unless its exact bytes are cryptographically authenticated back to the publisher-verified package.

Filesystem ownership, timestamps, inode metadata, and an unchanged source-package SHA-256 are useful operational signals but SHALL NOT substitute for cryptographic integrity of the bytes actually interpreted by the scanner.

This should be treated as a scanner/package-runtime security requirement, not merely a performance optimization.
