issues.title: [M2] Open-source SCAP-NG repository normalizer for shared Assessment reuse
issues.body:
## Purpose

Create an open-source SCAP-NG **repository normalizer** intended to run periodically against a native NG content-development repository.

Its primary job is to identify Assessment implementations that are semantically equivalent, promote one canonical copy into the repository's shared-Assessment area, and update every Rule reference to the shared Assessment without changing assessment semantics.

This is an authoring/repository-maintenance utility, not a scanner feature.

## Required behavior

The normalizer SHALL:

1. Discover native SCAP-NG Benchmark, Rule, Policy, Assessment, applicability, profile/tailoring, and shared-Assessment files using the current authoring contracts rather than filename guessing alone.
2. Resolve Rule → Assessment references using the same relative-path semantics required by the SCAP-NG authoring model.
3. Compare Assessments by **semantic content**, not by filename, formatting, YAML key order, comments, or source path.
4. Detect duplicate/equivalent Assessments within one benchmark and across multiple benchmarks in the repository.
5. Produce a dry-run report describing:
   - equivalence groups,
   - current source paths and logical IDs,
   - all Rules that reference each Assessment,
   - the proposed canonical shared Assessment,
   - references that would be rewritten,
   - any provenance/metadata differences that prevent safe automatic normalization.
6. When rewrite mode is explicitly requested, move/promote the canonical Assessment into the repository's shared-Assessment area and update all authoring references atomically.
7. Preserve stable logical Assessment identity where possible. File paths SHALL NOT be treated as semantic identity.
8. Preserve or merge provenance without silently discarding source attribution.
9. Re-run repository reference validation after rewriting and fail without committing partial changes if any reference is unresolved or any semantic identity conflicts.
10. Be deterministic and idempotent: a second run against an already-normalized repository SHALL produce no further changes.
11. Support a CI/report-only mode suitable for periodic GitHub Actions execution.
12. Never merge Assessments merely because their human-readable titles, Rule IDs, filenames, or check text happen to match.

## Near-duplicate review candidates

In addition to exact semantic deduplication, the normalizer SHOULD identify
**near-duplicate Rules and Assessments for human review**.

This mode is advisory only. It SHALL NOT automatically merge or rewrite content
unless full Assessment semantic equivalence has been proven.

Useful review candidates include cases where:

- two Rules have substantially equivalent policy intent, identifiers,
  discussion/check/remediation text, platform scope, or parameter structure,
  but reference different Assessments;
- two Assessments differ in only a small number of semantic nodes, such as one
  predicate, collection path, variable, operator, or platform-specific detail;
- equivalent Rule intent across different STIGs appears to have independently
  developed automated Assessments;
- one Rule is manual while a substantively similar Rule elsewhere has an
  automated Assessment that may be reusable after author review;
- two implementations appear structurally similar but differ enough that the
  tool cannot prove equivalence.

The report SHOULD explain *why* each pair/group was considered similar and
SHOULD surface the exact semantic differences. Similarity scoring MAY help rank
review candidates, but a similarity score SHALL NOT be treated as proof of
semantic equivalence.

The normalizer SHOULD distinguish at least three outcomes:

1. **equivalent** — safe candidate for automatic shared-Assessment
   normalization;
2. **near duplicate / review suggested** — potentially reusable, but requires
   author analysis;
3. **different** — no normalization action.

Near-duplicate discovery SHOULD consider Rule metadata separately from
Assessment semantics. Similar Rule text or identifiers can be a useful signal
for review, but SHALL NOT justify an automatic Assessment merge.

## Semantic-equivalence requirements

The equivalence fingerprint should be computed from a canonical semantic representation of the Assessment. It should ignore serialization-only differences such as YAML key ordering, whitespace, comments, file paths, and other non-semantic authoring presentation.

The fingerprint SHALL include all fields capable of changing execution or result truth, including at minimum:

- Assessment mode/class/purpose where semantically relevant;
- test logic and Boolean structure;
- collections/objects and their effective attributes;
- states/predicates and effective/default attributes;
- variables and the complete variable dependency graph;
- sets and filters;
- external/organizational inputs and binding semantics;
- existence and quantifier semantics;
- behaviors;
- applicability semantics where part of the Assessment;
- evidence/result-affecting controls that change evaluation semantics.

The utility SHALL NOT automatically merge two Assessments when equivalence cannot be proven.

## Provenance and metadata

Two semantically equivalent Assessments may have different legacy source Rule IDs, STIG references, benchmark origins, titles, or migration provenance. Those differences should not necessarily prevent sharing, but they MUST NOT be lost.

Repository normalization should keep Rule-specific policy metadata with the Rule layer and retain multi-source Assessment provenance in an appropriate non-semantic provenance structure.

If provenance cannot be combined without ambiguity, report the candidate but do not rewrite automatically.

## Canonical shared placement

The exact shared directory naming convention should follow the final native source-layout decision, but the normalizer should conceptually transform:

```text
benchmark-a/.../assessments/foo.assessment.yaml
benchmark-b/.../assessments/bar.assessment.yaml
```

into one canonical shared Assessment, for example:

```text
shared/assessments/<stable-name>.assessment.yaml
```

with the referring Rule files rewritten to their new relative paths.

The shared filename SHOULD be stable and deterministic, preferably derived from a reviewed logical identity rather than from whichever duplicate happened to be discovered first.

## Safety / review workflow

Default mode SHOULD be dry-run/report-only.

Rewrite mode SHOULD:
- operate on a clean working tree or explicitly record pre-existing changes;
- write all changes as one coherent transaction;
- validate the complete repository after normalization;
- provide a machine-readable change manifest;
- make it straightforward to review the resulting Git diff or use the tool from an automated pull-request workflow.

## Relationship to existing work

This supports but is distinct from:
- #19 four-anchor benchmarks and evidence-based cross-STIG Assessment reuse;
- #24 native authoring workflow;
- package/runtime manifest resolution.

The normalizer operates on the **authoring repository**. Runtime package manifests remain compiler-generated and are not an author-maintained Assessment index.

## Open-source deliverable

Provide the utility under the repository's open-source tooling area with:
- CLI help and examples;
- dry-run and rewrite modes;
- deterministic semantic fingerprint documentation;
- unit tests for true duplicates, near-duplicate Rule/Assessment review candidates, and unsafe-to-merge cases;
- repository-scale regression tests;
- GitHub Actions example for periodic duplicate/reuse reporting.

issues.title: [M1] Define detailed SCAP-NG Assessment, Test and collected-item JSON result schemas
issues.body:
## Goal

Define the developer-facing SCAP-NG analog of OVAL Results + OVAL System Characteristics without reproducing legacy XML/ARF nesting.

## Proposed schema family

- `scan-result.schema.json`: run/target/Benchmark/Profile/Tailoring identity, summary and Rule-result references.
- `rule-result.schema.json`: policy-facing Rule outcome, applicability, effective Assessment selection, deterministic message/reason and decisive evidence references.
- `assessment-result.schema.json`: detailed Assessment/Test execution graph, Test outcomes, Collection outcomes, variable bindings, completeness and diagnostics.
- `collected-item.schema.json`: typed observed items/entities with capability identity, item status, typed field values/statuses and collection provenance.
- `result-types.schema.json`: reusable result enums, completeness, identifiers, typed values, diagnostics and references.

## Required semantics

1. Preserve distinct truth/result values: true, false, error, unknown, not_evaluated, not_applicable. Do not collapse to Boolean.
2. Preserve evaluation layers independently: Collection/exists status, State/entity/variable aggregation, per-item State results, Test state_operator, Test check and final Test result.
3. Preserve Collection status/flags and completeness, including complete/incomplete/error/not-collected/not-applicable/does-not-exist analogs where semantically required.
4. Collected items are reusable first-class result objects; Tests reference them rather than requiring repeated embedding.
5. Item entities/fields carry datatype, value, status and masking/redaction metadata where relevant. Missing required evidence must not be represented by fabricated items.
6. Variable bindings retain datatype, one-or-many values, source/provenance and error/unknown status where applicable.
7. Evidence caps and early termination must preserve logical_complete, population_complete, evidence_complete and truncation/count semantics.
8. Rule results remain compact and self-describing for SIEM use while detailed developer results remain available through references.
9. Canonical package may be normalized; JSONL/Splunk projections are downstream views and must not dictate the canonical model.
10. Schema versioning must be explicit and independently version the result format from the content schema/package format.

## OVAL crosswalk to cover

- oval-results: Test result, tested_item, tested_variable, criteria/result status.
- oval-system-characteristics: collected_object flags, object/item references, item status, entity status/value/mask.
- OVAL Definitions controls required to explain result aggregation: check_existence, check, state_operator, State operator, entity_check, var_check.

## Open design questions

- Whether Test/State/Collection result nodes are embedded under one Assessment result or normalized into separate arrays keyed by stable execution IDs.
- Exact typed-value JSON representation for scalar, record and multi-valued entities.
- Whether complete scan packages embed all collected items or permit a separate evidence member referenced by digest.
- How much of the decisive evaluation tree is mandatory versus debug/full-detail mode.
- Stable identifiers for runtime execution instances when one Assessment/Test is evaluated repeatedly with different parameter/variable bindings.

## Acceptance

Versioned draft JSON Schemas plus RHEL9 and Windows examples, schema validation tests, OVAL-results/System-Characteristics crosswalk, bounded-evidence examples, and at least one existence, one multi-State, one multi-variable and one collection-error worked result.

This work complements `specification/results/results.md`; it does not replace the higher-level Benchmark/Rule result model.

comments.body:
Result-retention decision point: must a canonical Assessment Result retain all evaluated Items, or may a scanner retain only failures?

Recommended direction:

### Canonical detailed Assessment Result
If an Assessment Result reports `population_complete: true`, it SHOULD retain all collected/evaluated Items that materially participated in the Assessment, not only failing Items.

Rationale:
- a passing Test may depend on the fact that every observed Item satisfied State requirements;
- retaining only failures makes a successful evaluation impossible to audit from the result itself;
- it weakens the meaning of `population_complete` because the result no longer contains the population it claims was completely evaluated;
- future imported/shared-Item semantics are cleaner when the consuming Assessment Result contains the observations it actually used;
- deterministic re-analysis/debugging is possible without recollecting the target.

### Failure evidence is a separate bounded projection
`evidence.failures` identifies the bounded subset of Items most useful for explaining a failure. It does not define the complete Item store.

Illustrative:
```yaml
evaluation:
  population_complete: true
  evaluated_items: 34

items:
  # all 34 evaluated Items

evidence:
  failures:
    maximum: 50
    returned: 3
    item_refs: [item-sync, item-shutdown, item-halt]
```

### Compact/retention profile
A scanner MAY support an explicit compact result mode that retains only decisive/failing evidence or otherwise prunes Item bodies, but the result MUST declare that fact. It SHALL NOT claim a full canonical detailed result while silently discarding evaluated passing Items.

Possible metadata:
```yaml
retention:
  item_mode: failures_only   # or all_evaluated / decisive_only
  source_population_complete: true
  retained_item_count: 3
  evaluated_item_count: 34
```

Important distinction:
- `population_complete` describes how much of the target population was evaluated;
- `evidence_complete` describes whether configured evidence-retention obligations were satisfied;
- Item-retention mode describes how much of the evaluated observation set was serialized.

These are independent axes and should not be conflated.

comments.body:
Filter semantics for Assessment Results:

Agreed design direction: the Item population represented in a canonical Assessment Result is **post-filter**.

Example:
- Object selection: collect files matching `.*`;
- Filter: retain only files that are world-readable;
- Result Item population: only the files that survive the filter.

Consequences:
- `evaluated_items`, Object `item_count`, Test `item_refs`, and retained Item bodies SHALL be counted from the post-filter population that actually participates in Test evaluation;
- pre-filter candidate objects/items are collector/intermediate state and SHALL NOT be presented as the Assessment's evaluated Item population;
- `population_complete` refers to complete evaluation of the effective post-filter population, not merely complete enumeration of raw candidates;
- failure counts and evidence maximums operate on the post-filter/evaluated population;
- a filter that excludes an Item means that Item does not participate in the Test result and ordinarily does not appear in the canonical Assessment Result.

Potential optional diagnostic/debug mode:
A scanner MAY retain pre-filter collection statistics or trace records for troubleshooting, but those records must be clearly labeled as collection/filter diagnostics and must not be mixed with canonical evaluated Items.

Illustrative:
```yaml
object_result:
  collection_status: complete
  raw_candidate_count: 1240        # optional diagnostic
  post_filter_item_count: 17
  item_refs: [item-1, ... item-17]

filter_diagnostics:
  excluded_count: 1223             # optional
```

Important semantic distinction:
`Object` describes the effective object-selection semantics, including filters. `Item` represents an observation that survived those semantics and was available to Test evaluation.

This should be carried into the OVAL->NG terminology/schema mapping so filters are not treated as an after-the-fact result decoration.

issues.body:
## Scope
Follow-up to #10 and #11, distinct from enterprise performance (#29) and the reference scanner (#26).

The variable-depth review found that static concat allocated a Cartesian product before checking its 4096-value ceiling. Native lowering also relied on recursive Python calls: a finite acyclic chain could exceed host recursion and raise an exception. Immediate fixes are being prepared: concat cardinality preflight, native resource-limit diagnostic with no partial Assessment, cycle guards and iterative feature accounting.

## Remaining work before claiming unbounded graph support
- Define and expose converter budgets separately for dependency nodes/edges, expression nesting, generated output expansion, candidate values, string/value bytes and elapsed work. Do not choose normative numerical thresholds without evidence.
- Specify diagnostics that distinguish invalid reference/cycle, unsupported semantics, and implementation/resource exhaustion. A valid source exceeding a host limit is not thereby invalid OVAL.
- The feature checker can traverse a long DAG iteratively, but native lowering and some static evaluation remain recursive. Replace remaining recursive conversion paths where practical, or explicitly expose their limits and prevent uncaught exceptions.
- Measure repeated/shared Collection lowering. Inlining a shared graph can duplicate work/output; optimize only when native sharing semantics and error/evidence behavior are established. Do not change the native source architecture solely for convenience.
- Test a deep single-valued chain independently of a shallow high-cardinality product; test wide shared DAGs, nested sets/functions, zero values, and failure isolation.
- Keep computation budgets separate from evidence caps; preserving the source AST is mandatory when optional static evaluation is bounded.

## Acceptance
Documented limits and repeatable adversarial fixtures; no silent truncation, approximate pass, or complete-looking partial Assessment. A deterministic blocker identifies the affected unit and resource. Preserve existing finite supported source behavior. Any proposed native/runtime outcome or Board cycle policy remains clearly pending review.

Educational impetus: coworker modernization draft plus an unconfirmed three-layer scanner failure. No scanner defect is diagnosed without a reproducer.

## Immediate safeguards landed
[Commit df915611](https://github.com/vanderpol/scap-ng/commit/df915611a61c1535d42b56fc2d90e057c93a85c6) is on main: indexed iterative feature accounting, static concat cardinality preflight, Variable/Object cycle guards, and conversion_resource_limit:python_recursion with no partial native Assessment. issues.title: [M2][Research, non-voting] Canonical execution JSON and multiple authoring presentations: fidelity prototype
issues.body:
**Status: Research / prototype — NOT an OVAL Board voting question.**
**Roadmap relationship:** M2 specification and authoring alternatives (#25); depends on native split Rule → Policy → Assessment contract (#31), fidelity gates (#7–#11) and a stable canonical execution model.

## Question
Can the full Rule/Policy/Assessment, compact Rule/Assessment, and restricted Ansible-inspired assessment presentations compile to one canonical, versioned SCAP-NG execution JSON representation without losing assessment or policy semantics?

## Distinguish two fundamentally different propositions
A. **Multiple source layouts for the same native assessment language.** Full split source has explicit Policy; a compact Rule/Assessment source can synthesize an explicit, fully validated Policy/check-selector representation. This is primarily source/reference resolution and normalization.

B. **A distinct Ansible-inspired source language.** This requires actual semantic translation and poses substantially greater risk. No general-purpose Ansible interpreter, module execution or command injection should be assumed. Some constructs must fail closed rather than be approximated.

## Critical risk / failure mode
STIG requirements may be correct, the source author may describe those requirements correctly, the scanner may correctly execute its compiled JSON, *and yet the compliance finding may be wrong because the compiler changed the intended semantics*. Syntax-valid JSON, identical round trips, or source compiler self-comparison cannot alone prove behavior.

## Proposed bounded prototype (research only)
1. Define **candidate canonical JSON IR** representing named check selections/default selector, applicability, parameters, manual checks, automated assessment graphs, variable dependencies, statuses, evidence limits, reuse and provenance without source file-path coupling. Source links compile to stable IDs; preserve relevant full policy context for reporting.
2. Start with 5–10 independently hand-reviewed cases: file exists/does-not-exist, Test vs State entity existence, var_check and repeated entities, recursive sets/filters, manual assessment, applicability, tailored/default/alternate named check selectors, and multi-rule assessment reuse.
3. Author equivalent behavior in full Rule/Policy/Assessment and compact Rule/Assessment; demonstrate canonical JSON equivalence *after deterministic normalization*, retaining explicit selector semantics, diagnostics and mapping.
4. Evaluate an Ansible-inspired **restricted** representation separately. Reject unsupported/ambiguous operations; do not implicitly support arbitrary Ansible playbook capabilities.
5. Test against **independent expected outcomes** for known evidence fixtures and, where feasible, differential execution with a separately implemented evaluator. Round-trip compare and schema validation are necessary but insufficient.
6. Preserve a debug trail: source file/line, expanded construct, compiled JSON node/ID, compiler version and source/compiled digest, and scanner result/evidence correlation. Demonstrate how to localize an intentionally introduced compilation defect.
7. Measure implementation complexity, unsupported feature rate, compiler diagnostics, conversion errors and additional runtime/packaging cost. Keep normative canonical contract separate from authoring-profile conveniences.

## Gates before an OVAL Board discussion or vote
- No new normative language or board vote yet. First publish tested examples, scope boundaries, assurance evidence, maintainability tradeoffs and remaining incompatible semantics.
- Ask owner to review a concise comparative demonstration; then create a clearly marked **non-voting discussion** for early feedback.
- Only formulate a separately labeled voting proposal when board members have sufficient evidence and the owner requests it.
- Do not divert work from currently higher-priority hidden-default, NIWC corpus and Self-Assertion fidelity tasks.

**Success is not three formats compiling without errors; it is independent evidence that equivalent source intentions yield equivalent scanner behavior with diagnosable failures.**

comments.body:
Deferred conditional-evaluation design discussion — illustrative only, no implementation yet.

The current unresolved topics in this issue already include runtime notapplicable and short-circuit behavior. A related question is whether SCAP-NG should have an explicit conditional construct analogous to if / else-if / else.

## Proposed scope boundary

Conditional evaluation SHOULD NOT be an applicability-only feature.

Applicability Assessments should remain ordinary native Assessments used by an applicability consumer. If SCAP-NG adopts conditional evaluation, the same primitive can be used in:
- applicability Assessments;
- ordinary configuration/compliance Assessments;
- potentially manual/organizational-input Assessments where appropriate.

The difference is how the caller interprets the Assessment result, not a separate conditional language.

For example:
- applicability consumer: true -> applicable; false -> not applicable;
- ordinary compliance Rule: true -> pass; false -> fail;
- error/unknown retain their normal assessment semantics.

Do not add a general-purpose scripting language. Every branch, Test, Collection, Variable and action-capable capability SHALL be statically declared in the signed Assessment. A condition may select among already-declared evaluation branches; it SHALL NOT construct shell commands, SQL, paths, capability names, file references or arbitrary executable content dynamically.

## Small illustrative examples

These examples are intentionally schematic and are NOT accepted syntax.

### 1. Applicability Assessment

A Server 2025 rule that applies only to domain controllers:

```yaml
assessment:
  id: example.server2025.dc-applicability
  mode: automated

  tests:
    is-server-2025:
      ...
    is-domain-controller:
      ...

  evaluate:
    if:
      test: is-server-2025
    then:
      test: is-domain-controller
    else: false
```

The applicability consumer interprets true as applicable and false as not applicable. Unknown/error remain explicit.

### 2. Ordinary compliance Assessment with alternatives

```yaml
assessment:
  id: example.crypto-policy
  mode: automated

  tests:
    fips-enabled:
      ...
    fips-policy-correct:
      ...
    normal-policy-correct:
      ...

  evaluate:
    if:
      test: fips-enabled
    then:
      test: fips-policy-correct
    else:
      test: normal-policy-correct
```

This is an ordinary compliance Assessment. The conditional chooses the appropriate already-declared evaluation branch.

### 3. Else-if chain

```yaml
evaluate:
  if:
    test: is-domain-controller
  then:
    test: dc-setting-correct
  else_if:
    - if:
        test: is-member-server
      then:
        test: member-setting-correct
  else:
    result: not_applicable
```

This raises an important design question: should an ordinary Assessment be permitted to emit runtime not_applicable, or should applicability always be separated before Rule evaluation?

## Recommended semantic direction for debate

1. Conditional logic should operate on Assessment evaluation, not arbitrary authoring-time preprocessing.
2. Conditions should consume already-defined Test results, Variables/typed inputs, or other explicitly permitted immutable values.
3. All possible branches must be statically visible to schema/compiler/signature validation.
4. No branch may synthesize executable strings or dynamically choose unsigned/unlisted capabilities.
5. else should be explicit when omission would make the outcome ambiguous.
6. Error/unknown propagation must be defined. A failed condition evaluation cannot silently behave as false unless the specification explicitly says so.
7. Short-circuit behavior must be defined separately from logical meaning. Runtime MAY avoid executing an unused branch if no other Assessment requires its Collections/Tests, but shared Collection dependencies must prevent one consumer's short-circuit from suppressing data another consumer requires.
8. Result output should record which branch was selected and why.
9. Conversion from SCAP 1.4 SHALL NOT invent conditional constructs merely for optimization. Use them only where needed to preserve actual source semantics or in future native authoring.

## Question to resolve before adding syntax

The major architectural choice is whether conditional evaluation is truly needed as a first-class construct or whether existing declarative Boolean logic plus explicit applicability Assessments can represent the same semantics cleanly.

If conditionals are adopted, prefer a constrained declarative case/when model over a programming-language-like if/elseif/else surface if that makes evaluation/result semantics clearer.

No schema or converter changes should be made yet.
comments.author: vanderpol

comments.body:
Follow-up refinement: conditional evaluation must be able to consume an existing authored Applicability Assessment result without duplicating its Tests/Collections.

Historical content has valid cases of the form:

`if <applicability assessment X is true> then evaluate A else evaluate B`

The native model SHOULD support this directly.

Illustrative only:

```yaml
assessment:
  id: example.config-check

  dependencies:
    - assessment: ../applicability/server-role.assessment.yaml
      as: server_role

  tests:
    dc-setting-correct:
      ...
    member-setting-correct:
      ...

  evaluate:
    if:
      assessment_result: server_role
      equals: true
    then:
      test: dc-setting-correct
    else:
      test: member-setting-correct
```

The exact syntax is not decided. The semantic requirement is the important part:

1. Applicability logic is authored once.
2. Another Assessment may reference/consume that Assessment's result as a conditional input.
3. The consuming Assessment SHALL NOT need to duplicate the referenced Assessment's Tests, Collections, Variables, or criteria.
4. The dependency is statically declared and resolved by the compiler; runtime SHALL NOT load arbitrary external content.
5. The referenced Assessment result preserves the full native result domain. `error`, `unknown`, and `not_applicable` SHALL NOT be silently coerced to false.
6. Result dependency is distinct from Collection reuse. The consumer may need only the referenced Assessment's final result, not its internal observations.
7. Compiler/runtime cycle detection is required because Assessment-result dependencies create an execution DAG.
8. If the referenced Applicability Assessment is already required elsewhere in the same scan, its execution result SHOULD be reused rather than evaluated twice.

This creates a useful distinction:
- applicability relationship: a Rule/Benchmark uses an Assessment to decide whether it applies;
- result dependency: an Assessment consumes another Assessment's result in its own evaluation;
- Collection reuse: an Assessment consumes observations gathered by another/shared Collection execution.

These mechanisms may interact but are not the same feature.

This also argues that conditional evaluation should not be restricted to inline Tests. Conditions should be permitted to reference statically declared Assessment-result dependencies.

No implementation/schema change yet.
comments.author: vanderpol

comments.body:
Further clarification: conditional evaluation should preserve BOTH of these valid forms as first-class use cases.

### A. Branch on a local Test result

Example semantics:
`if local-test == true then evaluate test-A else evaluate test-B`

This is useful when the branching condition is naturally part of the same Assessment and does not warrant a separate reusable Assessment.

Illustrative only:

```yaml
evaluate:
  if:
    test: fips-enabled
  then:
    test: fips-policy-correct
  else:
    test: normal-policy-correct
```

### B. Branch on another Assessment's result

Example semantics:
`if applicability-assessment-X == true then evaluate test-A else evaluate test-B`

This is useful when the condition is already authored as a reusable Applicability/Assessment and should not be duplicated.

Illustrative only:

```yaml
evaluate:
  if:
    assessment_result: server-role
    equals: true
  then:
    test: dc-setting-correct
  else:
    test: member-setting-correct
```

These capabilities SHOULD NOT be collapsed into one by forcing authors to:
- create a separate Assessment for every local branch condition; or
- duplicate an existing applicability Assessment's logic inside a consuming Assessment.

Design requirement: a future conditional construct should be able to consume at least:
- local Test results;
- statically declared dependent Assessment results.

Potentially later it may also consume typed Variables/inputs, but that should be decided separately.

The same non-Boolean-result rule applies to dependent Assessments: error/unknown/not_applicable need explicit semantics and must not silently collapse to false.

No implementation/schema changes yet.
comments.author: vanderpol

comments.body:
Conditional-evaluation conversion boundary — current design conclusion:

- Conditional evaluation is a potential native SCAP-NG feature.
- Ordinary SCAP 1.4 -> SCAP-NG conversion SHALL NOT invent or opportunistically introduce conditional constructs merely because equivalent content could be expressed more elegantly with them.
- Existing conversion output should remain unchanged when current NG Boolean/applicability semantics already preserve the source behavior.
- Native content authors MAY use conditional evaluation once/if the feature is standardized.
- The normalizer SHALL NOT rewrite converted Assessments into conditional form as an optimization.
- The compiler/runtime SHALL support conditional constructs when they are explicitly present in valid native content.
- The only exception for conversion is semantic necessity: if a legacy construct is discovered whose behavior cannot be preserved faithfully without the NG conditional construct, the converter MAY/SHALL emit it as required for lossless semantics. That use must be evidenced by a concrete source case and regression tests rather than convenience.

This keeps the feature effectively silent for legacy imports until native authors choose to use it, while leaving a narrow path for lossless migration if future corpus analysis proves it necessary.

Current conditional scope under discussion remains:
- branch on a local Test result;
- branch on a statically declared dependent Assessment result, including an existing Applicability Assessment;
- possible future typed Variable/input conditions, to be decided separately;
- no general scripting/dynamic command construction;
- all branches and dependencies statically declared and signed;
- explicit semantics still needed for error/unknown/not_applicable, short-circuiting, result explanation, dependency cycles, and shared Collection interactions.

No schema/converter/runtime implementation changes are authorized by this discussion yet.

comments.body:
Terminology reconsideration: `Collection` vs OVAL-aligned `Object`.

A practical reviewer/content-author concern is emerging: SCAP-NG currently preserves a large majority of OVAL's conceptual model, but renaming OVAL `Object` to authored `Collection` forces experienced users to constantly translate terminology when discussing converted and native content.

Unless there is a concrete semantic benefit that justifies the divergence, the native terminology SHOULD align with established OVAL names.

Proposed distinction for debate:

- **Object** — authored declarative description of what system data is requested/selected. This aligns with OVAL Object semantics.
- **Item** — an actual collected observation/instance produced from evaluating an Object against a target. This also aligns with OVAL/System Characteristics terminology.
- **Test** — evaluates the Items associated with an Object against State requirements / test semantics.
- **State** — expected/required characteristics used in Test evaluation.
- **Variable** — retain OVAL-aligned terminology where semantics remain substantially equivalent.
- **Collection / collection execution** — runtime operation that evaluates an Object and produces Items. This is an execution/result concept, not necessarily an authored top-level construct.

Conceptually:

```text
Authored:
  Test -> Object -> State

Runtime:
  Object
    -> collection execution
       -> Item(s)
    -> Test evaluates Item(s) against State
```

This would let future collection-reuse work speak precisely about a **shared collection execution of an Object** rather than redefining the Object itself as a Collection.

Benefits:
1. Reduces terminology translation for existing OVAL/SCAP authors and scanner developers.
2. Makes SCAP 1.4 -> NG conversion easier to review because Test/Object/State/Variable names remain recognizable.
3. Keeps the native divergence budget focused on places where NG really changes semantics instead of merely renaming familiar constructs.
4. Clarifies the runtime-reuse discussion: Objects are authored definitions; collection executions and Item sets are runtime instances.
5. Makes the glossary/crosswalk simpler and reduces repeated `Collection/Object` explanations.

Potential downside to evaluate:
- `object` is generic terminology in JSON/programming contexts, so schemas/documentation must clearly define `Object` as the SCAP-NG assessment concept rather than an arbitrary JSON object.

That ambiguity may be smaller than the ongoing human cost of renaming a retained OVAL concept.

Because the project is still pre-alpha, now is the right time to decide this before schemas, examples and authoring guidance make `Collection` entrenched.

No rename is being implemented by this note; treat it as a terminology/design decision to resolve deliberately.

comments.body:
Terminology principle refinement:

While terms such as `Object` and `check` can feel overly generic, they have roughly two decades of established meaning in the OVAL/SCAP community. If SCAP-NG intentionally retains the majority of OVAL's conceptual model, preserving those established names may materially reduce the cognitive and adoption burden for the OVAL Board, scanner implementers, and experienced content authors.

Proposed principle:

> **If SCAP-NG retains an OVAL construct with substantially the same semantics, retain the established OVAL term unless there is a clear semantic or usability benefit that outweighs the compatibility cost.**

Conversely:

> **If SCAP-NG later makes a fundamental architectural break from an OVAL construct, that is the appropriate point to introduce a deliberately new vocabulary rather than incrementally renaming familiar concepts while preserving their semantics.**

This avoids an awkward middle state where SCAP-NG is structurally OVAL-like but uses enough renamed concepts that experienced users must constantly translate terminology mentally.

Practical implication for current discussion:
- Test -> keep `Test` if semantics remain recognizably OVAL Test semantics.
- Object -> prefer `Object` over authored `Collection` if it remains the declarative data-selection construct.
- State -> keep `State` if semantics remain recognizably OVAL State semantics.
- Variable -> keep `Variable` if semantics remain substantially equivalent.
- Item -> keep `Item` for runtime observations where the concept still matches OVAL/System Characteristics.
- Collection / collection execution -> reserve for the runtime process of gathering Items from an Object, especially when discussing reuse/caching.

This is not an instruction to preserve every historical OVAL term forever. It is a migration/adoption principle: either preserve familiar terminology while preserving the model, or, if the model is eventually replaced, introduce a coherent new vocabulary at that point rather than piecemeal.

No implementation rename yet; resolve during the terminology/schema pass.

comments.body:
Assessment vocabulary alignment checkpoint before deep capability-schema generation.

Current generated automated Assessments use a surface such as:

```yaml
checks:
  some-check:
    test_title: ...
    capability: ...
    collect:
      object_title: ...
      capability: ...
      select: ...
    assert:
      existence: ...
      check: ...
      state_operator: ...
      states:
        - state_title: ...
          capability: ...
          state: ...
evaluate:
  check: some-check
```

This means the terminology review is broader than only `Collection` -> `Object`. Before generating deep schemas from OVAL XSD/Schematron, explicitly map the native vocabulary to retained OVAL concepts and decide each divergence deliberately.

Working principle:
> If the native construct remains substantially the same OVAL concept, prefer the established OVAL term. If SCAP-NG intentionally changes the concept, use a new term and document the divergence.

Likely retained concepts to review first:
- OVAL Definition -> SCAP-NG Assessment (intentional higher-level rename; likely retain Assessment)
- OVAL Test -> current generated `checks.<name>` / check node
- OVAL Object -> current generated `collect` / earlier `Collection` terminology
- OVAL State -> current generated `assert.states[]` / State
- OVAL Variable -> current Variable
- OVAL Test `check` -> current assertion/check aggregation term
- OVAL `check_existence` -> current `existence`
- OVAL `state_operator` -> current `state_operator`
- OVAL State entity `entity_check` -> current `entity_check`
- OVAL State entity `var_check` -> current/inherited var-check semantics
- OVAL criteria/criterion -> current Assessment `evaluate` expression
- OVAL System Characteristics Item -> current Item/result observation

Intentional terminology improvements that SHOULD remain unless a concrete problem is found:
- OVAL `comment` -> typed descriptive fields `test_title`, `object_title`, `state_title`, `variable_title`;
- OVAL Definition metadata title -> `assessment_title`;
These are not arbitrary renames: `comment` is semantically vague, while the typed title fields identify the node being described and are useful to authors, reviewers, and generated documentation.

Do not start deep generated capability schemas until this mapping is reviewed, because generated schema property names would otherwise bake in vocabulary we may immediately rename.

Deliverable for this checkpoint should be a compact terminology table with columns:
`OVAL term | current SCAP-NG term | proposed SCAP-NG term | semantics retained? | reason for divergence | migration mapping`.

After terminology is settled, capability-schema generation can use that mapping as an explicit input rather than infer names ad hoc.

comments.body:
Evaluate/criteria clarification:

`evaluate` must preserve the full logical expressive power of OVAL criteria trees, including arbitrarily nested AND/OR groupings and leaf Test references. The name `evaluate` is a native terminology improvement; it is not intended to reduce semantics.

Lossless migration requirement:
- OVAL `criteria` logical groups map to nested `evaluate` logical groups;
- OVAL `criterion` Test references map to leaf Test references;
- nesting depth SHALL NOT be arbitrarily limited by the SCAP-NG language;
- grouping/order/negation semantics, where present in the source, SHALL be preserved;
- the converter SHALL NOT flatten a tree when flattening would alter semantics or provenance;
- a scanner MAY internally normalize/compile the tree into another execution representation (e.g. DAG/bytecode) provided the result semantics remain identical.

Illustrative native shape only:

```yaml
evaluate:
  all:
    - test: test-a
    - any:
        - test: test-b
        - all:
            - test: test-c
            - test: test-d
```

This can represent the same kind of deep/binary logical structures that legacy OVAL authors create, without retaining XML `criteria`/`criterion` serialization.

Important design principle:
> We may simplify the syntax and improve readability, but lossless conversion requires preserving logical structure even when the source structure is complex or awkward.

Potential later authoring improvements can include canonical formatting, flattening associative groups where provably equivalent, visual/tree tooling, and linting against needlessly deep trees. Those are authoring/normalization conveniences, not reductions in language capability.

No arbitrary maximum nesting depth should be introduced merely to simplify the schema or evaluator.

comments.body:
Assessment authoring simplification decision candidate:

**Containment implies private scope; IDs imply referenceable scope.**

SCAP-NG SHOULD permit Objects and States to be embedded directly in a Test when they are private to that Test. Embedded/private nodes do not require authored IDs and cannot be referenced outside their containing Test. Components that are reused or externally referenced remain named top-level Objects/States.

This also creates a useful normalization rule for converted OVAL content:
- if a Test references an Object used by exactly that Test, and the Object is not independently referenced by a Variable/set/filter or other node, the normalizer MAY inline it into the Test;
- if a State is used only by that Test (or by an inline filter owned by that private Object), the normalizer MAY inline it as well;
- shared/referenced Objects and States remain named nodes;
- normalization must preserve source/provenance mappings even when a source OVAL ID no longer appears as a native authored ID.

For the common 1 Test -> 1 Object -> 1 State graph, the result is a single readable Test rather than three top-level registries. This is a semantic-preserving authoring simplification, not a loss of Object/State concepts.

Assessment Results can identify private inline nodes by deterministic structural identity/path derived from the containing Test; an authored ID is not required solely for result traceability.

This should be evaluated alongside filter scoping, because the same design principle applies: private contained nodes are structurally scoped; named nodes exist when independent reference/reuse is required.

comments.body:

comments.body:
2026-10-02 design clarification — clean break from legacy schema baggage:

Native SCAP-NG capability schemas SHALL be designed as a clean native model. OVAL/XCCDF/SCAP 1.4 are semantic migration and conformance references, not naming/inheritance/serialization templates.

Practical consequences:
- Do not copy OVAL type hierarchies, attribute-group structure, legacy enum spellings, or deprecated vocabulary into native NG merely for familiarity.
- Preserve behavior that current content or validation material actually requires, but express it using the simplest coherent NG vocabulary.
- Deprecated OVAL values remain importer errors/migration diagnostics; they do not become native enum members.
- OVAL defaults are importer semantics. Native authored NG continues to expose behavior-affecting values explicitly rather than reproducing hidden legacy defaults.
- Shared NG concepts should be defined once in reusable common schemas even when their source semantics were scattered across multiple OVAL XSD types.
- Names may deliberately differ from OVAL where the NG name is clearer (for example the already adopted State-entity `entity_existence` distinction).
- Source XSD/Schematron details and old identifiers belong in crosswalk/provenance documentation, not in the native runtime contract.
- Do not add compatibility aliases to native content unless there is a concrete interoperability requirement approved later.

This supersedes any interpretation of the earlier capability-schema plan that would mechanically reproduce OVAL common enums/types. The generator may learn semantics from pinned OVAL, but its output should be clean native SCAP-NG.

comments.body:
Additional reuse evidence for the clean-break capability model:

Pinned independent definitions repeat the same file-selection/traversal semantics across `filehash`, `filehash58`, `textfilecontent54`, `xmlfilecontent`, and `yamlfilecontent`: filepath vs path+filename selection, max-depth/recurse controls, filesystem-scope controls, and the same cross-field restrictions. This confirms file selection/traversal belongs in one native shared primitive, not in each capability schema.

`capability-common.schema.json` now contains clean native shared primitives (`58a001d`), including comparison operations, match quantifiers, existence requirements, logical operators, native datatype vocabulary, and a reusable downward-only `file_selection` / `file_traversal` model. The shared model intentionally omits legacy recurse-direction because upward traversal was deprecated baggage.

Windows file-family binding will be done from its authoritative pinned source when located; do not infer Windows-specific junction/reparse behavior from memory. comments.body:
Clean-break legacy-design correction ledger (first unix.file pass):

These are intentional native fixes, not compatibility gaps:

- OVAL `recurse_direction`: upward traversal was deprecated/unused; native file traversal is downward-only and has no direction field.
- OVAL `max_depth=-1`: replace magic sentinel with `max_depth: null` for unlimited and non-negative integers otherwise.
- OVAL `recurse` string enum: replace with explicit `follow_symlinks: boolean`; directories are intrinsic to downward traversal rather than an enum choice.
- OVAL `recurse_file_system=all|local|defined`: native `filesystem: any|local|same`.
- Hidden OVAL behavior defaults: native behavior-affecting settings are explicit; importer materializes effective legacy defaults.
- OVAL `filepath/path/filename`: native `full_path/directory/name`; directory-self selection is `name: null`, not XML nil semantics.
- XML `xsi:nil` / `nil`: not a native Assessment concept.
- OVAL operation spellings (`equals`, `pattern match`, etc.): map to concise native comparison operations (`equal`, `match`, etc.).
- OVAL quantifier spellings (`at least one`, `only one`, `none satisfy`): native `any|one|none`; deprecated `check='none exist'` remains a migration error.
- OVAL existence names: native cardinality-oriented `all|some|none|one|optional`, with error/unknown/completeness propagation defined separately.
- OVAL `any_exist` misleading semantics: represented as native `optional`, not carried forward by name.
- OVAL broad string/int allowances for UNIX UID/GID and epoch-time fields: native fields are integer-only because the semantic values are numeric; conversion handles legacy lexical forms.
- OVAL single-letter permission fields (`uread`, `gwrite`, etc.): native descriptive names (`owner_read`, `group_write`, etc.).
- OVAL `suid/sgid`: native `setuid/setgid`.
- OVAL XSD substitution/type hierarchy and Schematron placement: not reproduced. JSON Schema handles local structure; semantic validation handles graph/cross-field rules.
- OVAL Set `COMPLEMENT`: native `difference`; native Set/filter structure is shared across capabilities instead of copied through XSD families.
- OVAL shared entity defaults such as `mask=false`: native authored content is explicit where behavior/results can change.
- Legacy source field/type metadata stays in migration mappings/evidence, not generated runtime capability schemas.

Open design item, not yet finalized: UNIX permission representation. Current native names are clearer, but we should still decide whether individual booleans remain the best long-term representation or whether a compact permission/mode structure gives a simpler scanner/author experience without harming lossless conversion.

comments.body:
Second capability clean-break finding (`independent.filehash58`):

The OVAL Object `hash_type` entity is semantically different from filepath/path/filename selectors: it instructs the scanner which digest algorithm to compute. Native SCAP-NG should not preserve the fiction that every Object child is the same kind of comparison entity.

Proposed native separation:
- `select`: identifies system resources/items (shared file selection/traversal primitive);
- `collect`: capability-specific collection parameters that control what data is gathered but do not select the target resource;
- State/expected-value fields remain assertions against collected item properties.

For native file hashing this points toward an Object shape conceptually like:

```yaml
select:
  full_path: ...
collect:
  algorithm: sha256
```

instead of wrapping `algorithm` in value/operation/datatype/mask simply because OVAL modeled `hash_type` as an Object entity.

Legacy values MD5/SHA-1/SHA-224/SHA-256/SHA-384/SHA-512 should be translated to a native normalized algorithm vocabulary (likely lowercase `md5`, `sha1`, `sha224`, `sha256`, `sha384`, `sha512`). The empty-string legacy enum exists only for XML variable-reference mechanics and should not enter native content.

`windows_view` in the filehash58 State is explicitly deprecated in the pinned 5.12.3 source and should not enter the native file-hash capability.

Before finalizing this second capability, audit real corpus use of State `hash_type` to determine whether native State needs an independently assertable algorithm field or whether algorithm identity is already fully determined by the Object collection parameter and collected evidence.
comments.author: vanderpol

comments.body:
Reusable capability pattern emerging from file.hash/text/XML/YAML review:

Native Object semantics should distinguish three concerns instead of treating every source Object child as the same entity shape:

1. `select`: identifies which system resources/items are in scope.
2. `traversal`: controls how a selector expands through a resource hierarchy when applicable.
3. `collect`: capability-specific instructions controlling what data is gathered or computed from selected resources.

Examples:
- `unix.file`: file selection + optional traversal; no extra collection parameter.
- `file.hash`: shared file selection/traversal + `collect.algorithm`.
- future text-file capability: shared file selection/traversal + text pattern/query collection parameters.
- future XML capability: shared file selection/traversal + XML query collection parameter(s).
- future YAML capability: shared file selection/traversal + YAML query collection parameter(s).

This is an intentional correction to the OVAL Object model, where selectors and collection instructions are often both represented as entity-like children with operation/datatype/variable machinery even when those semantics do not fit the field.

The generator now supports mapping-declared native collection parameters (`8614f29` + `5c63ea4`), and `file.hash` is the first proof of that separation (`78b3f7c`, tests `5a663b9`/`5e8a25b`).

comments.body:
Windows file-family clean-break findings:

- Exact Windows OVAL 5.12.3 definitions schema is now pinned in scap-ng from scap-content, byte-for-byte identical (`5403ea1`, identical blob SHA `b32c4a414a648b67e2796dd6b8c7dc822d1f6318`).
- Shared native file traversal was corrected from Unix-specific `follow_symlinks` to platform-neutral `follow_links` (`2b86569` plus dependent test/doc updates). Windows junction/reparse-style link traversal and Unix symlink traversal map to the same high-level native intent.
- Windows OVAL `recurse_direction='up'` is explicitly deprecated in the pinned 5.12.3 schema for the same reason as Unix: unused and unnecessary interpreter complexity. Native traversal remains downward-only with no direction field.
- Windows `windows_view` behavior/state is explicitly deprecated in the pinned source and is omitted from native `windows.file`.
- Native `windows.file` reuses the same full_path vs directory+name selector model, traversal model, Set/filter model, comparison/entity semantics, quantifiers, and existence semantics as unix.file/file.hash.
- Windows-specific file type and file attribute enums are normalized to simple lowercase native values instead of preserving Win32 constant spellings.
- Windows c_time semantics are creation time, not Unix inode-change time, so native mapping uses `creation_time` rather than reusing the Unix `change_time` name.
- Literal Windows file-name reserved-character validation remains a Windows-specific semantic rule; match expressions are exempt.

This gives us a useful proof that the shared file-selection/traversal model is semantic rather than Unix-specific.
comments.author: vanderpol

comments.body:
Clean-break checkpoint — windows.registry and direct Variable-backed Tests:

**windows.registry**
- Added reusable `hierarchy_traversal` (`max_depth: integer|null`, downward-only). Registry uses this without file-specific `follow_links` or filesystem scope.
- Native registry selection is explicit at all hierarchy levels: `hive`, `key`, `name`.
- `key: null` means the hive itself; `name: null` means the key itself; `name: ""` is intentionally distinct and means the registry default value.
- Registry hive is a simple normalized selector (or Variable reference), not a generic comparison entity; arbitrary pattern/ordering operations on HKEY constants are not meaningful.
- Hive constants normalize to `classes_root`, `current_config`, `current_user`, `current_user_local_settings`, `local_machine`, `users`.
- Registry type aliases are collapsed: `reg_dword_little_endian` -> `dword`, `reg_qword_little_endian` -> `qword`; other REG_* spellings map to concise native values.
- `windows_view` and upward recursion are omitted because the pinned 5.12.3 source explicitly deprecates them.
- Exact literal registry type States constrain value datatype only where semantics are unambiguous (for example dword/qword -> integer, binary -> binary, REG_SZ/string -> string or version). Pattern/Variable/multiple-type cases are intentionally not guessed.

**variable.value**
- The OVAL `variable_object -> var_ref -> variable` indirection is not native SCAP-NG.
- A `variable.value` Test references a named Variable directly through `variable`.
- No native Object definition is emitted for this capability.
- OVAL `variable_state/var_ref` is redundant identity plumbing and is omitted; the native State predicate is only `value`.
- Automated Assessments now omit unused `objects`/`states` node families instead of requiring empty placeholders.
- Capability mappings now declare Test source kind; Object-backed Tests remain first-class where resource selection exists, but Object is not a universal Test wrapper.
- Variable/State datatype compatibility is deliberately deferred until the native Variable schema itself is stabilized; current contract validates direct Variable reference existence only.

These changes are intentional fixes to legacy schema architecture, not conversion losses. Importers carry the source crosswalk and produce the simpler native graph.

issues.title: [M1] Manual questions, organizational inputs, tailoring and provenance
issues.body:
**Proposed milestone:** M1; **status:** open; **track:** SCAP-NG roadmap.

Design policy-only/manual questions from DISA Check Text, typed organizational data when requirements are unknown, test-selector selection, external tailoring versus interactive runtime input, and approval metadata. User-controlled values SHALL NOT dynamically select tests or inject commands; result stores value/approval provenance. **Done:** schemas, valid/invalid examples and tests in RHEL/Windows cases; documented SCAP 1.4 compatibility and deviations. **Dependencies:** #12.

**Evidence required for closure:** implementation references, passing focused checks and conformance/quality limits; include blockers in issue comments. See `ROADMAP.md`.

comments.body:
Organizational Input is now active design work. Current direction:

1. Separate the **publisher declaration** from the **organization-supplied values**.
   - Benchmark Parameter declares identity, type/cardinality, prompt/description, constraints, requiredness, and `resolution: organization`.
   - External Organizational Input Set supplies values and provenance.
2. Organizational Input does not Tailor or rewrite publisher policy. It is legal only where the publisher explicitly leaves a Parameter unresolved.
3. An Assessment Request explicitly binds the Organizational Input Set. Scanners SHALL NOT implicitly select one by filename, hostname, organization metadata, local convention, or target matching.
4. An Input Set is bound to an exact Benchmark identity/version. It may carry intended-scope metadata for human/governance use, but scope metadata does not cause implicit application.
5. Effective values are validated against the publisher Parameter type/cardinality/constraints before execution, then frozen for the run.
6. Missing required Organizational Input produces `not_evaluated`/equivalent with a structured missing-input reason, not pass/fail and not not-applicable.
7. Provenance distinguishes organization, supplied_by/supplied_at, optional authorization/approval, source system/import, and value-level provenance where needed.
8. Persistent Input Sets may be reused across runs only through explicit request binding. Per-run interactive/API values are another allowed supply channel but receive the same validation/provenance treatment.
9. Values SHALL NOT alter Assessment selection, Tests, Objects, collection behavior, operators, commands, privileges, or other executable semantics.

This work also retires the older example behavior that treated Tailoring as a Parameter-override mechanism.
comments.author: vanderpol

comments.body:
Organizational Input design refinement under active review:

Current preferred direction is **publisher-authored State completion**, not arbitrary Assessment mutation.

The Assessment fixes the executable semantics: selected Assessment, capability, Object, Test, check_existence, check, state_operator, State structure, operators, datatypes, entity_check/var_check, etc. The publisher may leave only explicit value-bearing State slots unresolved.

An Organizational Input declaration names those unresolved slots. A scanner can derive a UI/API input contract from the capability-specific State schema plus the slot metadata, require all mandatory values, validate supplied values, and materialize the complete State JSON before Test evaluation.

Potential shape:
```yaml
states:
  approved-time-source:
    state_title: Configured source is organization approved
    capability: linux.chrony
    hostname:
      operation: equals
      datatype: string
      value:
        organizational_input: approved_time_sources
```

The organization supplies only:
```yaml
values:
  approved_time_sources:
    - ntp1.example.test
    - ntp2.example.test
```

Important constraints to preserve:
- Organizational Input may fill only explicitly declared unresolved value slots.
- It cannot change the Object, Test, State operator, datatype, operation, check/check_existence, filters, commands, privileges, or other executable semantics.
- The completed State must validate against the same generated capability schema as a fully publisher-authored State.
- One Organizational Input value may need to feed more than one State slot/Assessment, so named reusable input identity is still useful.
- Missing required input => not_evaluated/missing_organizational_input, never guessed.
- Input provenance remains independent of Tailoring.

Open design question: whether the named Organizational Input contract lives at Benchmark level and is referenced from State slots, or whether State slots themselves are sufficient declaration and the Benchmark merely inventories them. Avoid finalizing until reuse, multi-field States, optional fields, and shared Assessments are pressure-tested.
comments.author: vanderpol

comments.body:
Key design refinement: Organizational Input is an **organization-authorized policy assertion**, not merely a typed value.

For each value, the model should be able to preserve organization, supplier, authority/policy basis, authorization reference, approver, supplied/authorized timestamps, intended scope, effective/expiration dates, source system, optional POC, and supersession/change provenance.

Supplier, authority, and approver are distinct roles. Per-value provenance is required when values in one Input Set come from different authorities. Results should be able to answer: what value was used, who/what asserted it, under what authority, for what scope, and when it was effective.

Remediation use is intentionally not part of this decision; Organizational Input here remains focused on completing delegated expected-state data for assessment.
comments.author: vanderpol

comments.body:
Defined end-to-end Organizational Input provenance propagation:

`Input Set/runtime entry -> frozen effective policy -> Benchmark Result provenance registry -> Assessment Result consumed bindings -> Rule Result assessment_result_ref -> optional SIEM denormalization`

The Benchmark Result carries the authoritative run-local snapshot and full provenance/authority for each effective Organizational Input assertion. Each assertion gets a stable result-local reference. Assessment Results record only the inputs/state slots they consumed, effective value (or redacted representation), materialization/validation status, and the provenance reference. Rule Results normally reach that through the Assessment Result instead of duplicating the authority record. Standalone SIEM events may denormalize it while preserving canonical IDs.

This gives compact canonical results and still supports independent aggregator events.
comments.author: vanderpol

comments.body: Refined result propagation: because Rule Results are embedded in the Benchmark Result and are the primary policy-facing records, any Rule evaluated with Organizational Input now exposes the effective organization-defined value(s) directly. Each value also carries a stable reference to the canonical Benchmark-result provenance assertion, with an optional compact provenance summary. Full authority/contact provenance remains normalized once at Benchmark-result level.
comments.author: vanderpol

comments.body:
Result-model refinement to avoid SCAP 1.4-style hidden/rare fields:

- Every embedded Rule Result now SHALL contain `expected_state`, even for ordinary fully publisher-authored automated checks.
- Organizational Input uses the same expected-state structure; it only changes `source` and adds a provenance reference.
- Manual/procedure-only rules still carry `expected_state: []` when no materialized State applies.
- This prevents consumers from treating Organizational Input as a rare optional extension they never programmed for.
comments.author: vanderpol

comments.body:
Formalized Organizational Input conformance behavior:

- Every Rule exposes `organizational_input_requirements` (empty when none), mapped by Assessment choice for up-front discoverability.
- Scanner result metadata declares `capabilities.organizational_input`.
- Unsupported capability -> `not_evaluated / unsupported_organizational_input`.
- Supported but required value missing -> `not_evaluated / missing_organizational_input`.
- Supplied value invalid -> `not_evaluated / invalid_organizational_input`.
- Valid input -> normal Assessment execution.
- `expected_state` remains present in every Rule Result.
- JSON Schema constrains the common result shape/reason vocabulary; semantic validation is still required for reference resolution, Rule/Assessment contract agreement, and capability-specific State validation.
comments.author: vanderpol

comments.body:
Refined multi-Test Organizational Input addressing.

Rule-level discoverability now identifies each consumer as `Assessment choice -> Test ID -> State ID -> State slot/entity`, not just by input name. This covers Assessments with multiple Tests, shared/reused States, multiple organization-resolved fields in one State, one input reused by multiple Tests, and multiple inputs consumed by one Test.

The Rule record remains a compiler-verified discovery index; the Assessment State is authoritative.
comments.author: vanderpol

comments.body: Related design: Issue #53 distinguishes Organizational Input from post-assessment Deviation/adjudication. Org Input resolves expected policy State before execution; Deviation preserves the actual automated result and records an authorized disposition afterward.
comments.author: vanderpol

comments.body: Manual interaction follow-up is tracked in Issue #54. The key boundary remains: typed Manual answers are target observations supplied during assessment; Organizational Input supplies organization-authorized expected policy State. Do not merge those concepts.

comments.body:
Design correction from owner review — Collection capability/type must remain first-class.

We previously moved toward a single authoritative Test capability with Collection/State inheriting it. That is too restrictive for the accepted reusable-Collection model.

Revised direction:
- A named Collection is an independently meaningful/reusable dependency node and therefore SHALL carry its own capability/type describing acquisition semantics and the shape of collected items.
- A Test SHALL carry its own evaluation capability/contract describing what item/predicate semantics it can evaluate.
- A Test MAY reference one or more compatible Collections; compatibility SHALL be validated explicitly rather than inferred by filename or inherited blindly.
- The same Collection MAY be reused by multiple compatible Tests and Variables.
- Collection capability and Test capability will often match, but equality SHALL NOT be assumed as the only valid relationship unless the capability contract specifically requires it.
- State/predicate compatibility remains independently validated. Converter/runtime code SHALL NOT overwrite Collection/State type identity with the Test type merely to make content fit.
- This preserves the NGINX lesson where Test/Object/State type mismatch was a real source defect that schema validation alone did not catch.
- Native authoring SHOULD avoid redundant type noise where references make compatibility obvious, but it must not make a standalone Collection uninterpretable outside a Test.

Need follow-up changes to current examples/spec/schema where Collection capability was removed or described as inherited-only.
